evidence.snippet: Microarray analyses showed overlapping 6q deletions, extending from 92 138 719 bp to 108 227 875 bp (hg19).
evidence.explanation: The cohort includes variable overlapping intervals; these coordinates describe the combined span, not a recurrent deletion.

evidence.snippet: The 6q16.1 deletions segregated with the phenotype in multiplex families and were shown to be de novo in four families
evidence.explanation: Documents both familial transmission and de novo occurrence.

steps/3.description: A variable interstitial deletion removes one copy of the genes within its specific boundaries. No single gene is deleted in every interval represented here; de novo and inherited events occur.

evidence.snippet: Except for patients no. 14 and 15, all patients had deletions that included the SIM1 gene.
evidence.explanation: SIM1 involvement is determined by deletion boundaries; it is absent from two intervals in this cohort.

evidence.snippet: only 8 of 13 patients with SIM1 deletion exhibited obesity, in agreement with incomplete penetrance of SIM1 haploinsufficiency.
evidence.explanation: The authors interpret variable obesity as incomplete penetrance. The cohort includes a fetus and the tables have discrepant obesity totals, so this quoted count is not used as a penetrance estimate.

steps/4.description: Loss of one SIM1 copy is an established genomic finding in a subset of 6q16 deletions. Human deletion cohorts and separate intragenic-variant studies support an incompletely penetrant contribution to obesity.

evidence.snippet: We found a strong loss-of-function effect of p.T46R, p.H323Y, and p.T714A mutations on SIM1 transcriptional activity with both ARNT and ARNT2
evidence.explanation: Reporter assays establish variant-specific loss of transactivation in engineered human cells, not hypothalamic histology in deletion carriers.

steps/5.description: Selected obesity-associated SIM1 variants reduce ARNT- and ARNT2-dependent reporter activation. These experiments support loss of transcription-factor function as a mechanism; they do not demonstrate loss of hypothalamic neurons or a particular target-gene defect in deletion carriers.

evidence.snippet: The six families described in the report by Kasher et al. had the deletion of the POU3F2 and FBXL4 genes, although the deletion size was different in each family
evidence.explanation: Identifies both genes in the overlapping interval; these are not POU3F2-only deletions.

evidence.snippet: In an international collaboration, we identified ultra-rare truncating and missense variants in another ten individuals sharing autism spectrum disorder, NDD, and adolescent-onset obesity.

steps/6.description: SIM1-sparing 6q16.1 deletions remove one POU3F2 copy together with FBXL4 and, depending on their extent, additional genes. Subsequent intragenic-variant evidence strengthens POU3F2 as a contributor without making the whole chromosomal disorder monogenic.

evidence.snippet: Except for a variant leading to early truncation of the protein, identified variants showed adequate nuclear translocation but overall disturbed DNA-binding ability and promotor activation.
evidence.explanation: Functional summary from the available abstract of the intragenic-variant study. Effects differ by variant and are not measurements in deletion-carrier hypothalamus.

steps/7.description: Reported POU3F2 variants disturb DNA binding or promoter activation, with nuclear translocation retained except for the early-truncating variant. The transcriptional consequences of heterozygous deletion in human brain remain incompletely measured.

evidence.explanation: Persistent expressive-language delay in the reported child. The edge represents a clinical developmental association; the quote does not resolve its cellular intermediates.

edges/20.description: Language delay is a documented component of the variable neurodevelopmental phenotype; the responsible neural intermediates remain unresolved.

evidence.snippet: She could walk at the age of 2 years and 4 months and could speak meaningful words at 2 years and 9 months.
evidence.explanation: Documents separate motor and speech milestones. The edge represents a clinical developmental association; the quote does not resolve its cellular intermediates.

edges/21.description: Delayed acquisition of walking is a motor-developmental manifestation in the detailed SIM1-sparing case; a specific central motor lesion has not been established.

evidence.snippet: She revealed hypotonus, an attenuated deep tendon reflex in both lower limbs, and autistic features.
evidence.explanation: The source describes autistic features, not a formally assessed ASD prevalence. The edge represents a clinical developmental association; the quote does not resolve its cellular intermediates.

edges/22.description: Autistic features are documented in the SIM1-sparing case, without a standardized autism diagnosis or a resolved cellular pathway.

evidence.snippet: In our study, three of eight patients having behavioural disorders (patient no. 3, 13, and 14) were not deleted for GRIK2.
evidence.explanation: The prose confirms behavioral disorders in this cohort while illustrating that GRIK2 deletion does not explain every affected individual. No disease-wide frequency or single-gene attribution is inferred. The edge represents a clinical developmental association; the quote does not resolve its cellular intermediates.

edges/23.description: Clinical cohorts support behavioral involvement as part of the neurodevelopmental spectrum, with heterogeneous deletion content and incompletely identified mediators.

evidence.snippet: She showed strabismus, cleft soft palate, and hypotonia in the neonatal period.
evidence.explanation: Neonatal findings in one SIM1-sparing 780-kb deletion case. The edge represents a clinical developmental association; the quote does not resolve its cellular intermediates.

edges/24.description: Hypotonia accompanies developmental impairment in some deletion carriers. A central developmental contribution is plausible but not localized by the available clinical evidence.

evidence.snippet: In conclusion, our study suggests EPHA7 deletion should be con- sidered as a risk factor for NDD combining ID, behavioral disorders, speech delay and microcephaly with variable expressivity and incom- plete penetrance.
evidence.explanation: The expanded EPHA7 cohort supports a susceptibility phenotype; this is the authors' interpretation. Full-text source: Levy et al., EPHA7 haploinsufficiency is associated with a neurodevelopmental disorder (PMID:34176129; DOI:10.1111/cge.14017). The edge represents a clinical developmental association; the quote does not resolve its cellular intermediates.

edges/25.description: Some EPHA7-containing deletion carriers have postnatal microcephaly. The association with altered neurodevelopment is clinically supported without a demonstrated human cellular growth mechanism.

evidence.snippet: Except for patients no. 14 and 15, all patients had deletions that included the SIM1 gene.
evidence.explanation: SIM1 involvement is determined by deletion boundaries; it is absent from two intervals in this cohort.

evidence.snippet: We found a strong loss-of-function effect of p.T46R, p.H323Y, and p.T714A mutations on SIM1 transcriptional activity with both ARNT and ARNT2
evidence.explanation: Reporter assays establish variant-specific loss of transactivation in engineered human cells, not hypothalamic histology in deletion carriers.

evidence.snippet: Therefore, mutation of SIM1 is not always responsible for a fully penetrant form of obesity.
evidence.explanation: The study reports variable effects and variable clinical expression.

genes/0.notes: One contributor to obesity in SIM1-containing deletions. Strong loss-of-function intragenic variants support the gene assignment, but not all missense variants are damaging and obesity severity is incompletely penetrant. An intrafamilial odds ratio from selected variant carriers is not deletion-syndrome penetrance.

evidence.snippet: The six families described in the report by Kasher et al. had the deletion of the POU3F2 and FBXL4 genes, although the deletion size was different in each family
evidence.explanation: Identifies both genes in the overlapping interval; these are not POU3F2-only deletions.

evidence.snippet: In an international collaboration, we identified ultra-rare truncating and missense variants in another ten individuals sharing autism spectrum disorder, NDD, and adolescent-onset obesity.
evidence.explanation: Intragenic variants independently strengthen POU3F2 attribution; this is a separate monogenic cohort, not a deletion-syndrome frequency estimate.

evidence.snippet: Except for a variant leading to early truncation of the protein, identified variants showed adequate nuclear translocation but overall disturbed DNA-binding ability and promotor activation.
evidence.explanation: Functional summary from the available abstract of the intragenic-variant study. Effects differ by variant and are not measurements in deletion-carrier hypothalamus.

genes/1.notes: A supported contributor to neurodevelopmental impairment and obesity susceptibility in SIM1-sparing deletions. The overlapping 350-kb region also includes FBXL4; subsequent intragenic truncating and missense variants strengthen POU3F2 attribution. Functional effects are variant-specific. The separate monogenic cohort is not used to assign every finding or a frequency to chromosome-deletion carriers.

evidence.snippet: Four patients had tiny deletions involving only EPHA7
evidence.explanation: Single-gene deletions strengthen the locus association but the authors describe a susceptibility effect with incomplete penetrance. Full-text source: Levy et al., EPHA7 haploinsufficiency is associated with a neurodevelopmental disorder (PMID:34176129; DOI:10.1111/cge.14017).

evidence.snippet: The deletions were inherited in nine out of 12 patients, suggesting variable expressivity and incomplete penetrance.
evidence.explanation: The selected cohort supports variable expression; it does not estimate population penetrance. Full-text source: Levy et al., EPHA7 haploinsufficiency is associated with a neurodevelopmental disorder (PMID:34176129; DOI:10.1111/cge.14017).

evidence.snippet: Most deletions were inherited (9/12) from unaffected parent suggesting that haploinsufficiency of EPHA7 could act as a risk factor for NDD with variable expressivity and incomplete penetrance.
evidence.explanation: Discussion qualifies the risk-locus interpretation; family A had an affected father with a history of cranial concussion. Full-text source: Levy et al., EPHA7 haploinsufficiency is associated with a neurodevelopmental disorder (PMID:34176129; DOI:10.1111/cge.14017).

genes/2.notes: Partial or complete deletions support an incompletely penetrant neurodevelopmental susceptibility locus. Most deletions in the 2021 series were inherited, often from unaffected parents. A more severe case also had Williams-Beuren syndrome, and another had a larger deletion involving ZNF292; these are not clean EPHA7-only phenotypes.

evidence.snippet: Early identification of endocrine abnormalities can improve clinical outcome by allowing timely introduction of hormone replacement therapy.
evidence.explanation: Case-report recommendation tied to documented endocrine deficiency.

treatments/0.description: Replace deficient hormones when endocrine testing establishes a deficiency. The source provides a clinical rationale; it does not demonstrate a controlled treatment effect or prove a common hypothalamic lesion.

evidence.snippet: received physical therapy since age 6 months
evidence.explanation: Documents actual supportive care in one child, without comparative efficacy.

treatments/1.description: Physical therapy was used from infancy in the original EPHA7-containing deletion case with hypotonia and motor delay. The report does not quantify its treatment effect.

evidence.snippet: Surgical treatment for cleft palate was performed at 1 year and 3 months old.
evidence.explanation: Records actual case-specific treatment.

treatments/2.description: Surgical cleft-palate treatment was performed in one SIM1-sparing deletion case at 15 months. The causal relationship between the deletion and cleft palate was uncertain.

evidence.snippet: We found a strong loss-of-function effect of p.T46R, p.H323Y, and p.T714A mutations on SIM1 transcriptional activity with both ARNT and ARNT2
evidence.explanation: Reporter assays establish variant-specific loss of transactivation in engineered human cells, not hypothalamic histology in deletion carriers.

evidence.snippet: Using morpholino and mutant zebrafish models, we show that POU3F2 lies downstream of SIM1 and controls oxytocin expression in the hypothalamic neuroendocrine preoptic area.
evidence.explanation: Experimental pathway ordering and oxytocin-expression readout in zebrafish. The available abstract does not establish human neuron loss, circulating oxytocin deficiency or obesity rescue.

open_questions/0.rationale: SIM1 reporter loss, POU3F2 variant effects and zebrafish oxytocin-expression regulation support biological hypotheses. None establishes universal human paraventricular neuron loss, circulating oxytocin deficiency or a single causal route from the deletion to obesity and developmental impairment.

evidence.snippet: only 8 of 13 patients with SIM1 deletion exhibited obesity, in agreement with incomplete penetrance of SIM1 haploinsufficiency.
evidence.explanation: The authors interpret variable obesity as incomplete penetrance. The cohort includes a fetus and the tables have discrepant obesity totals, so this quoted count is not used as a penetrance estimate.

evidence.snippet: Four patients had tiny deletions involving only EPHA7
evidence.explanation: Single-gene deletions strengthen the locus association but the authors describe a susceptibility effect with incomplete penetrance. Full-text source: Levy et al., EPHA7 haploinsufficiency is associated with a neurodevelopmental disorder (PMID:34176129; DOI:10.1111/cge.14017).

evidence.snippet: The deletions were inherited in nine out of 12 patients, suggesting variable expressivity and incomplete penetrance.
evidence.explanation: The selected cohort supports variable expression; it does not estimate population penetrance. Full-text source: Levy et al., EPHA7 haploinsufficiency is associated with a neurodevelopmental disorder (PMID:34176129; DOI:10.1111/cge.14017).

open_questions/1.rationale: Intervals vary and some reported patients carry additional CNVs or large deletions. The 2015 series has inconsistent obesity totals between narrative and tables and includes a fetus among SIM1 deletions; the quoted 8/13 is not used as a penetrance estimate. The EPHA7 cohort includes unaffected transmitting parents and two severe cases with substantial alternative genetic contributions. These sources support qualitative variability rather than disease-wide frequency bands.

evidence.snippet: We identified a recurrent de novo mutation in TWIST2 in seven independent AMS-affected families, as well as another recurrent de novo mutation affecting the same amino acid in ten independent BSS-affected families.
evidence.explanation: The same allele recurs across unrelated AMS families.

evidence.snippet: She was known for AMS with the specific genetic mutation in the gene TWIST2 (c.223G > A), no pathogenic sequence changes were found in both her parents
evidence.explanation: Names the nucleotide change (c.223G>A) in an independently reported case.

evidence.snippet: a lysine at TWIST2 residue 75 resulted in AMS, whereas a glutamine or alanine yielded BSS
evidence.explanation: The residue-level genotype-phenotype correlation that separates this disorder from Barber-Say syndrome.

steps/1.description: A heterozygous substitution of lysine for the conserved glutamic acid at codon 75 of TWIST2 (NM_057179.2 c.223G>A), in the basic region of the bHLH domain that contacts DNA. It was the allele found in all seven AMS families of the gene-discovery series. Glutamine or alanine at the same residue gives Barber-Say syndrome instead, so the substituting amino acid, not only the position, sets the phenotype.

evidence.snippet: All identified mutations fell in the basic domain of TWIST2 and altered the DNA-binding pattern of Flag-TWIST2 in HeLa cells.
evidence.explanation: Direct measurement of altered DNA binding by the mutant proteins.

evidence.snippet: Our results suggest that autosomal-dominant TWIST2 mutations cause AMS or BSS by inducing protean effects on the transcription factor's DNA binding.
evidence.explanation: The authors' overall conclusion that altered DNA binding is the disease-relevant lesion; graded HUMAN_CLINICAL because it rests on the patient genetics as well as the cell assay.

evidence.snippet: ChIP-seq showed that the numbers of binding sites for p.Glu75Lys, p.Glu75Gln, p.Glu75Ala, and p.Gln77_Arg78dup TWIST2 were reduced compared to WT TWIST2 and that the mutants bound to many sites not shared with WT TWIST2.
evidence.explanation: Marchegiani et al. (2015), PMID:26119818, Figure 3B: reduced normal binding and mutant-only binding in HeLa cells.

evidence.snippet: Chromatin from HeLa cells overexpressing wild-type TWIST2 was subjected to ChIP-seq, identifying 630 DNA binding sites with a consensus sequence typical of an E-box motif.
evidence.explanation: Marchegiani et al. (2015), PMID:26119818, Figure 3A: the wild-type ChIP-seq comparison.

steps/2.description: In HeLa cells overexpressing tagged TWIST2, the disease alleles changed the genomic binding pattern relative to wild-type. Wild-type TWIST2 had 630 binding peaks with a canonical E-box consensus. Mutants, including p.Glu75Lys, retained only a fraction of wild-type peaks and bound additional sites. This supports both loss of normal binding and acquisition of abnormal binding; the relative contribution of each to human disease remains unresolved. The relevance to endogenous TWIST2 in craniofacial or dermal mesenchyme is provisional because the assay used overexpression in a cancer cell line.

evidence.snippet: TWIST2 encodes a basic helix-loop-helix transcription factor that regulates the development of mesenchymal tissues.
evidence.explanation: The developmental role of TWIST2 on which this node rests, stated as background in the abstract and naming no species, so graded OTHER.

evidence.snippet: Comparison of wild-type and mutant TWIST2 expressed in zebrafish identified abnormal developmental phenotypes and widespread transcriptome changes.
evidence.explanation: Transcriptional effect of the mutant proteins, including p.Glu75Lys, in zebrafish embryos.

evidence.snippet: Quantitative RT-PCR showed that twsit2 itself expression was indeed increased in homozygous embryos, and the proinflammatory cytokines, Il-1β and tnfa, were found highly expressed.
evidence.explanation: Expression changes in homozygous zebrafish carrying the AMS-equivalent knock-in (the source spells twist2 as "twsit2").

evidence.snippet: Gene ontology (GO) analyses revealed the greatest reduction in the expression of genes related to extracellular matrix (ECM), membrane components, and cytoskeleton
evidence.explanation: Marchegiani et al. (2015), PMID:26119818: RNA-seq of injected zebrafish embryos compared mutant with wild-type TWIST2 expression.

steps/3.description: Expression of the AMS p.Glu75Lys or Barber-Say p.Glu75Gln protein in zebrafish embryos changed the transcriptome relative to wild-type TWIST2 overexpression. The strongest decreases involved extracellular matrix, membrane and cytoskeletal gene sets. These are whole-embryo results, not a patient-mesenchyme transcriptome. Wild-type overexpression itself caused mild developmental defects, so dose and experimental context matter. Homozygous zebrafish carrying the equivalent knock-in allele also showed increased twist2 and pro-inflammatory cytokine expression.

evidence.snippet: Electron microscopy of skin biopsies of AMS-7.1 and AMS-7.2 showed thin, disrup- ted elastic ﬁbers with areas of amorphous deposits along abnormally oriented collagen ﬁbers and adjacent areas of microﬁbrillar proliferation
evidence.explanation: Marchegiani et al. (2015), PMID:26119818: direct ultrastructural findings in two affected family members. The PDF line-break hyphenation is retained.

evidence.snippet: Masson-Trichrome staining showed abnormal reticulodermal collagen pat- terns in AMS-7.1 and AMS-7.2 ... staining appeared within normal limits
evidence.explanation: Collagen organization was abnormal, whereas the elastic-fiber stain appeared normal; ultrastructure and routine staining are distinct readouts.

steps/4.description: Skin electron microscopy in affected individuals showed thin, elongated or disrupted elastic fibers, disordered collagen orientation and microfibrillar or amorphous deposits. Reticulodermal collagen staining was abnormal in AMS-7.1 and AMS-7.2, although elastic-fiber staining appeared normal. The tissue abnormality is directly observed; its precise causal relation to TWIST2 target-gene changes and the clinical skin phenotype remains provisional.

evidence.snippet: We report one more case showing that the condition is better described as a severe microblepharon because only the anterior lamella of the eyelids is shortened.
evidence.explanation: Oculoplastic characterisation of the lesion as anterior lamellar shortening.

evidence.snippet: Ablepharon-macrostomia syndrome (AMS) is a rare condition comprising severe deficiency of the anterior lamella of both eyelids, abnormal ears, macrostomia, anomalous genitalia, redundant skin, and absence of lanugo.
evidence.explanation: Defines the eyelid lesion as anterior lamellar deficiency.

evidence.snippet: The lids in AMS are not absent and should not be managed with complex reconstructive techniques.
evidence.explanation: Long-term surgical series concluding the lids are present but deficient.

evidence.snippet: This condition is characterized by redundant skin, low-set ears, macrostomia, ambiguous genitalia, and underdevelopment of the both upper and lower eyelids.
evidence.explanation: Both upper and lower lids are underdeveloped.

evidence.snippet: Abnormal development of the anterior lamella appears to be a common feature in all cases of AMS with mosaic expression.
evidence.explanation: The anterior lamellar defect persists in mosaic, milder cases.

steps/5.description:
The defining lesion. The eyelids are present but their anterior lamella (skin and orbicularis) is severely short, with shortening of the septum and levator aponeurosis also described, so the lids cannot cover the globe. Clinically this reads as ablepharon, and in milder or mosaic cases as short, hypoplastic lids. Oculoplastic reports stress that the lids are not truly absent, which is why grafting to lengthen the anterior lamella, rather than building a new lid, is effective.
PROVISIONAL because no study has traced p.Glu75Lys through eyelid morphogenesis; the link from TWIST2 to the eyelid is inferred from the phenotype and from where TWIST2 is expressed.

evidence.snippet: Twist2 knockdown on E13 left visible marks at the wound site, inhibited regeneration, and resulted in defective follicle formation.
evidence.explanation: Experimental loss of Twist2 in fetal mouse skin impairs hair follicle formation; the setting is wound regeneration, not development of the normal pelt.

evidence.snippet: Scalp hair is sparse in AMS only, but sparse eyebrows and eyelashes occur in both entities, and general hypertrichosis occurs in BSS.
evidence.explanation: The hair phenotype that this node is meant to explain, and its contrast with BSS.

evidence.snippet: Our knockout analysis reveals that twist2/dermo1 gene functions in the maintenance of the scale shape and organization during development as well as regeneration.
evidence.explanation: twist2 loss disturbs dermal skin appendages (scales) in zebrafish. INDIRECT because scales are not hair follicles and a knockout is not the human missense allele.

steps/6.description: Sparse or absent scalp hair, eyebrows, eyelashes and lanugo are consistent features of AMS and separate it from Barber-Say syndrome, in which the same residue substituted by glutamine or alanine gives generalized hypertrichosis. Twist2 is expressed in dermal mesenchyme and is required for normal hair follicle formation in mice, so impaired follicle induction is the most direct candidate mechanism. HYPOTHETICAL: no hair or scalp histology from an AMS patient has been reported, and the opposite hair phenotypes of the two allelic syndromes show that the lesion is not simple loss of TWIST2 function.

evidence.snippet: Interestingly, heterozygous mutants can survive to adults and be fertile, but most heterozygous adults showed the phenotypes of protruding jaw, unclosed mouth, and emaciated body at about 6 months
evidence.explanation: A heterozygous knock-in of the AMS-equivalent residue disturbs jaw and mouth morphology. INDIRECT because the fish jaw is not the human facial soft tissue and no eyelid or ear phenotype can be assessed.

steps/7.description: The facial gestalt - wide mouth with unfused commissures, first-degree microtia with low-set ears, depressed nasal bridge with underdeveloped alae, widely spaced eyes, flat or absent zygomatic arches and cheek pads at the mouth corners - is attributed to abnormal patterning of the TWIST2-expressing craniofacial mesenchyme. HYPOTHETICAL: this is the primary paper's stated rationale, supported in zebrafish only by non-specific head hypoplasia; the tissue-level mechanism of each feature is unstudied in AMS. The strongest model support is the heterozygous zebrafish twist2 p.Glu78Lys knock-in (the equivalent of human p.Glu75Lys), whose adults develop a protruding jaw and a mouth that does not close.

evidence.snippet: failure of lip fusion that results in an enlarged, fish-like mouth
evidence.explanation: States the causal relation between failed lip fusion and the wide mouth.

steps/8.description: The wide mouth of AMS is described as a failure of lip fusion at the lateral commissures. PROVISIONAL: based on clinical description, without imaging or histology of the perioral tissues.

evidence.snippet: In 60% of the cases, the lids were described as absent.
evidence.explanation: Literature review of 15 published patients; the basis for the FREQUENT band.

evidence.snippet: The ablepharon macrostomia syndrome is a severe congenital condition that includes total absence of the upper and lower eyelids
evidence.explanation: Early case description of apparently absent upper and lower lids.

evidence.snippet: Features of AMS include ablepharon, hypertelorism, macrostomia, dysplastic ears, sparse body hair, and ambiguous genitalia.
evidence.explanation: Ablepharon listed first among the features of AMS.

evidence.snippet: Small/absent eyelids 69/6 19/75 10–50 Corneal clouding 6 50 ?
evidence.explanation: De Maria et al. (2016), PMID:27196381. Table IV distinguishes small eyelids (19%) from absent eyelids (75%) in AMS.

steps/9.description: Apparently absent upper and lower eyelids at birth, with absent eyelashes; in fact severe shortening of the anterior lamella. The cornea is exposed from the first hours of life.

evidence.snippet: Ablepharon-macrostomia syndrome (AMS) is characterized by absent or short eyelids, macrostomia, ear anomalies, absent lanugo and hair, redundant skin, abnormal genitalia, and developmental delay in two-thirds of the reported patients.
evidence.explanation: Short rather than absent eyelids in part of the reported patients.

evidence.snippet: Mosaic expression of TWIST2 variants is correlated with a less severe phenotype than that reported for the typical expression of TWIST2 variants associated with BSS or AMS.
evidence.explanation: Mosaic individuals present at the milder end of the eyelid spectrum.

evidence.snippet: AMS-1.120 p.Glu75Lys M severe hypoplastic eyelids bilateral
evidence.explanation: Marchegiani et al. (2015), PMID:26119818. Table 1: severe bilateral eyelid hypoplasia in AMS-1.1. The attached 20 is the original-report citation marker.

steps/10.description: Short or hypoplastic lids (microblepharon) rather than apparent absence; the milder presentation, seen particularly in somatic mosaics.

evidence.snippet: Corneal clouding 6 50 ? Ectropion 81 94 ? Entropion — 6 10–50
evidence.explanation: De Maria et al. (2016), PMID:27196381. Table IV columns are BSS, AMS and Setleis syndrome; the AMS ectropion value is 94%.

evidence.snippet: anterior lamella causes ectropion, causing in turn lagophtalmus, which may need surgical correction
evidence.explanation: De Maria et al. (2016), PMID:27196381. The ocular discussion explicitly describes anterior-lamellar deficiency causing ectropion and then incomplete lid closure.

steps/11.description: Outward turning of the eyelid margin associated with anterior-lamellar underdevelopment. The accepted-case review recorded ectropion in 94% of its 16 AMS cases.

evidence.snippet: At long-term follow-up, all 3 cases who underwent upper eyelid lengthening with full thickness skin grafts placed over Müller muscle had clear corneas with a small amount of lagophthalmos.
evidence.explanation: Residual lagophthalmos after lid lengthening in three patients.

steps/12.description: Inability to close the eyes, present from birth until the lids are lengthened surgically; a small residual lagophthalmos persists after grafting in long-term follow-up.

evidence.snippet: Despite intensive ocular lubrication, severe exposure keratopathy developed within the first days after birth.
evidence.explanation: Neonatal exposure keratopathy despite lubrication.

evidence.snippet: Upon presentation, there was severe exposure keratopathy causing large bilateral sterile ulcers culminating in corneal melting of both eyes.
evidence.explanation: Severe exposure keratopathy progressing to ulceration in an infant.

steps/13.description: Exposure keratopathy from the uncovered cornea, developing within days of birth despite intensive lubrication in severe cases. It is the main threat to vision.

evidence.snippet: Timely intervention is critical to prevent exposure keratopathy, corneal ulceration, and permanent vision loss.
evidence.explanation: Names corneal ulceration as a complication of untreated exposure.

steps/14.description: Sterile corneal ulceration and melting from untreated exposure, which in one infant required bilateral penetrating keratoplasty.

evidence.snippet: Corneal opacities present initially improved in one eye, allowing a view of the pupil and a normal anterior chamber.
evidence.explanation: Corneal opacities in an infant with AMS, improving after lid reconstruction.

evidence.snippet: continuous exposure may cause corneal clouding occurring in half of the patients with AMS.
evidence.explanation: De Maria et al. (2016), PMID:27196381. The review explicitly reports corneal clouding in half of accepted AMS cases.

steps/15.description: Corneal opacities, which may improve after the lids are reconstructed.

evidence.snippet: Many have persistent visual problems, often related to early corneal exposure.
evidence.explanation: Historical clinically diagnosed series, including cases later excluded by the 2016 review; retained for descriptive context, not as the frequency denominator.

evidence.snippet: One such case is reported which illustrates the importance of immediate postnatal ocular management to minimise severe visual loss.
evidence.explanation: Severe visual loss as the outcome early management aims to prevent.

evidence.snippet: Visual impairments have been reported in almost one-third of patients. Photophobia may occur
evidence.explanation: De Maria et al. (2016), PMID:27196381. The ocular discussion reports visual impairment in almost one-third; this is a literature cohort, not a population estimate.

steps/16.description: Persistent reduced vision in many patients, usually attributable to corneal exposure in early life; prompt ocular protection and lid surgery are aimed at preventing it.

evidence.snippet: Ablepharon-macrostomia syndrome (AMS) is a rare condition comprising severe deficiency of the anterior lamella of both eyelids, abnormal ears, macrostomia, anomalous genitalia, redundant skin, and absence of lanugo.

evidence.snippet: Ablepharon-macrostomia syndrome (AMS) is characterized by absent or short eyelids, macrostomia, ear anomalies, absent lanugo and hair, redundant skin, abnormal genitalia, and developmental delay in two-thirds of the reported patients.

evidence.explanation: Flattened nasal bridge in a severely affected infant.

evidence.snippet: This patient had many dysmorphic features consistent with a severe phenotype of ablepharon-macrostomia syndrome (AMS) including a fish-like appearance of the mouth, rudimentary ears, absence of body hair, thin skin, absent nipples, abdominal distension, and genital abnormalities.
evidence.explanation: Thin skin in a severely affected infant.

evidence.snippet: Major facial characteristics present in both entities, albeit often in differing frequencies, are excessive facial creases, hypertelorism, underdevelopment of the anterior part of the eyelids (anterior lamella), ectropion, broad nasal ridge and tip, thick and flaring alae nasi, protruding maxilla, wide mouth, thin upper vermillion, and attached ear lobes.
evidence.explanation: Excessive facial creases among the major facial characteristics.

evidence.snippet: All identified mutations fell in the basic domain of TWIST2 and altered the DNA-binding pattern of Flag-TWIST2 in HeLa cells.
evidence.explanation: Links the basic-domain substitutions, including p.Glu75Lys, to altered DNA binding in a cell system.

edges/1.description: The substituted basic domain changes where TWIST2 binds the genome.

evidence.snippet: Comparison of wild-type and mutant TWIST2 expressed in zebrafish identified abnormal developmental phenotypes and widespread transcriptome changes.
evidence.explanation: Mutant TWIST2 changes developmental transcription in vivo. INDIRECT because it is overexpression in zebrafish embryos, not the heterozygous allele in human mesenchyme.

edges/2.description: Mutant-containing TWIST2 complexes are proposed to lose occupancy at normal targets or occupy new sites, altering downstream transcription. The effects in patient mesenchyme and the physiological balance of mutant and wild-type dimers remain unresolved.

evidence.snippet: Gene ontology (GO) analyses revealed the greatest reduction in the expression of genes related to extracellular matrix (ECM), membrane components, and cytoskeleton
evidence.explanation: Marchegiani et al. (2015), PMID:26119818: RNA-seq of injected zebrafish embryos compared mutant with wild-type TWIST2 expression.

edges/3.description: Reduced expression of extracellular matrix gene sets in mutant-expressing zebrafish and abnormal dermal matrix in affected people suggest a transcriptional route to the tissue lesion. Mediation by particular matrix genes has not been demonstrated in patient tissue.

edges/4.description: Disturbed TWIST2-directed mesenchymal development is inferred to underlie the eyelid malformation. No cited source demonstrates this step, and the stages of eyelid morphogenesis affected are not known.

evidence.snippet: Interestingly, heterozygous mutants can survive to adults and be fertile, but most heterozygous adults showed the phenotypes of protruding jaw, unclosed mouth, and emaciated body at about 6 months
evidence.explanation: The heterozygous AMS-equivalent knock-in disturbs jaw and mouth morphology in zebrafish. INDIRECT because the fish jaw is not the human facial soft tissue.

edges/5.description: The same disturbance is proposed to produce the facial patterning defects of the mouth, nose, ears and malar region.

evidence.snippet: In mice, Twist2 knockout reportedly caused progressive growth retardation, possibly as a result of upregulated cytokine signaling, leading to thin skin and sparse distorted hair follicles before death
evidence.explanation: Loss of Twist2 in mice gives sparse, distorted hair follicles. INDIRECT and BACKGROUND: it restates earlier knockout work in a paper about fetal wound healing, and a null allele is not the human heterozygous missense allele.

edges/6.description: Under the dominant-negative model, reduced effective TWIST2 activity in dermal mesenchyme would impair hair follicle formation, as Twist2 loss does in mice. This edge is a hypothesis: no study has examined hair follicles in AMS, and the allelic Barber-Say substitutions cause the opposite hair phenotype (hypertrichosis).

edges/7.description: Presumed tissue basis of lax, redundant skin; no study has tested the link directly.

edges/8.description: Presumed tissue basis of the thin skin.

edges/9.description: Presumed tissue basis of the excessive wrinkling.

edges/10.description: Severe anterior lamellar deficiency presents as apparently absent lids.

edges/11.description: Milder deficiency, particularly in mosaic individuals, presents as hypoplastic lids.

evidence.explanation: De Maria et al. (2016), PMID:27196381. The ocular discussion explicitly describes anterior-lamellar deficiency causing ectropion and then incomplete lid closure.

edges/12.description: Anterior-lamellar shortening causes outward turning of the lid margin.

edges/27.description: Unfused lateral commissures widen the oral aperture.

evidence.explanation: De Maria et al. (2016), PMID:27196381. The ocular discussion explicitly describes anterior-lamellar deficiency causing ectropion and then incomplete lid closure.

edges/28.description: Everted lids contribute to incomplete eye closure.

evidence.snippet: The most significant phenotypic presentation is rudimentary eyelids resulting in exposure keratopathy, corneal abrasions, and potential blindness.
evidence.explanation: States the causal route from deficient lids to exposure keratopathy.

edges/29.description: Incomplete lid closure exposes the corneal surface.

evidence.snippet: Upon presentation, there was severe exposure keratopathy causing large bilateral sterile ulcers culminating in corneal melting of both eyes.
evidence.explanation: States the causal progression in one patient.

edges/30.description: Unprotected exposure keratopathy progresses to sterile ulceration and melting.

edges/31.description: Ulceration heals with scarring and opacification.

evidence.snippet: We identified a recurrent de novo mutation in TWIST2 in seven independent AMS-affected families, as well as another recurrent de novo mutation affecting the same amino acid in ten independent BSS-affected families.
evidence.explanation: The recurrent de novo AMS allele across unrelated families.

evidence.snippet: She was known for AMS with the specific genetic mutation in the gene TWIST2 (c.223G > A), no pathogenic sequence changes were found in both her parents
evidence.explanation: An independently reported de novo c.223G>A case.

evidence.snippet: Mosaic expression of TWIST2 variants is correlated with a less severe phenotype than that reported for the typical expression of TWIST2 variants associated with BSS or AMS.
evidence.explanation: Somatic mosaicism gives a milder phenotype.

evidence.snippet: No mutation in either of these genes was found in a cohort of 11 patients with AMS from 10 unrelated families.
evidence.explanation: Before TWIST2 was identified, the Fraser syndrome genes (FRAS1, FREM2, GRIP1) and FRAS1 partners were excluded in a clinically diagnosed AMS cohort.

evidence.snippet: In all instances in which DNA was available from both unaffected parents, the TWIST2 mutation occurred de novo in the ﬁrst generation of individuals affected with AMS or BSS and was heritable in the third generation.
evidence.explanation: Marchegiani et al. (2015), PMID:26119818. Family sequencing supports de novo occurrence and subsequent transmission; the statement includes both allelic syndromes.

genes/0.notes: No ClinGen gene-disease validity assertion exists for TWIST2 and AMS (see the entry-level notes). No AMS-causing TWIST2 allele other than p.Glu75Lys was found among the references cited here.

evidence.snippet: Early amniotic membrane grafting may be done at the bedside and may help preserve the ocular in patients with severe eyelid deformities until more definitive treatment is performed.
evidence.explanation: Amniotic membrane grafting as a temporising measure.

evidence.snippet: Despite intensive ocular lubrication, severe exposure keratopathy developed within the first days after birth.
evidence.explanation: Lubrication alone failed to prevent keratopathy in a severe case, arguing against relying on it without early surgical cover.

evidence.snippet: A hard eye shield should also be placed over each eye to prevent contact of the corneal surface.
evidence.explanation: Protective shielding recommended in the accepted clinically diagnosed Feinstein report; molecular confirmation was not reported.

treatments/0.description: Urgent protection of the exposed cornea with intensive lubrication and a protective eye shield while arranging definitive lid reconstruction. A bedside amniotic membrane graft has been used as a temporary measure, although migration and corneal melting occurred in one severely affected infant. Lubrication alone may fail within days in severe cases.

evidence.snippet: Full thickness skin grafts placed over the inner aspect of the palpebral conjunctiva allow permanent eye protection.
evidence.explanation: Long-term outcome of anterior lamellar lengthening with skin grafts.

evidence.snippet: We report a new AMS case with a quantitative analysis of palpebral fissure changes following skin grafts over the upper and lower smooth tarsal muscles and lateral tarsorrhaphy.
evidence.explanation: Grafting over the tarsal muscles with lateral tarsorrhaphy.

evidence.snippet: In a secondary procedure at the adjusted age of 3 weeks, the flaps were partially divided, and visual input and development were successfully achieved, while maintaining corneal protection.
evidence.explanation: Masquerade flaps for temporary closure, then division for visual input.

evidence.snippet: We report a novel approach to multiplanar eyelid reconstruction in ablepharon-macrostomia syndrome involving use of a modified reverse hatchet flap in 1 lower eyelid along with division at the eyelid margin, recession of the eyelid retractors in conjunction with preputial skin grafting for anterior lamellar restoration in the other 3 eyelids.
evidence.explanation: Flap and preputial skin graft reconstruction.

evidence.snippet: The authors report the first case of autologous rib cartilage grafting and fat grafting for lower eyelid reconstruction in a patient with AMS.
evidence.explanation: Rib cartilage and fat grafting for the lower lid.

evidence.snippet: In one such patient we were able to reconstruct the eyelids in a three-stage procedure. Redundant skin from the retroauricular area was used to create full-thickness grafts.
evidence.explanation: Staged reconstruction with retroauricular full-thickness grafts.

evidence.snippet: Skin graft pigmentation in this black patient has been prevented by prolonged application of sun block.
evidence.explanation: Aftercare preventing graft hyperpigmentation.

treatments/1.description: Early surgery to cover the cornea, followed by lengthening of the deficient anterior lamella. Reported approaches include lateral tarsorrhaphy, full-thickness skin grafts from the retroauricular area or prepuce placed over the conjunctiva-Müller muscle complex or the smooth tarsal muscles, masquerade flaps to close the eyes temporarily, a modified reverse hatchet flap, and autologous rib cartilage with fat grafting for the lower lid. Grafts over Müller muscle gave clear corneas at 10-15-year follow-up with only minor lagophthalmos. Sun protection prevented graft hyperpigmentation in one patient with dark skin.

evidence.snippet: Extensive surgical reconstruction of both eyelids and bilateral penetrating keratoplasty was ultimately performed successfully to protect the ocular surfaces while trying to maximize the visual potential.
evidence.explanation: Keratoplasty with lid reconstruction after corneal melting.

treatments/2.description: Bilateral penetrating keratoplasty, combined with full-thickness lid reconstruction and temporary tarsorrhaphy, in an infant whose corneas melted from exposure; she tracked light binocularly at five and a half months. A salvage procedure reported once.

evidence.snippet: The child later underwent successful mouth reconstruction.
evidence.explanation: Surgical repair of the macrostomia.

evidence.snippet: The patient underwent 17 previously maxillofacial operations requiring intubation, including multiple surgeries for eyelids and ears lobes reconstruction, mastoplasty for mammary glands absence and lips correction.
evidence.explanation: The cumulative surgical burden in one adult with confirmed AMS.

evidence.snippet: In our opinion, such major proce- dures are best deferred until craniofacial growth is completed.
evidence.explanation: De Maria et al. (2016), PMID:27196381: timing advice for major elective reconstructive procedures in AMS and Barber-Say syndrome, not for urgent ocular protection.

treatments/3.description: Repair of macrostomia and individualized reconstructive procedures are reported. One adult with molecularly confirmed AMS had undergone 17 operations, including eyelid and ear-lobe reconstruction, lip correction and breast surgery. The 2016 review recommends an experienced multidisciplinary team and generally deferring major elective facial procedures until craniofacial growth is complete; urgent corneal protection is a separate priority.

evidence.snippet: The importance of paying particular attention to the management of both the physical appearance and the consequences of these entities on the quality of life is stressed by the affected individuals themselves.
evidence.explanation: Patient-reported priorities for psychosocial care.

evidence.snippet: Early and honest communication, adapted to the level of the child, has been performed, sometimes by treating physicians, sometimes by parents.
evidence.explanation: De Maria et al. (2017), PMID:28690482, Table 1: communication practices reported across the mixed AMS/Barber-Say sample.

evidence.snippet: surgical procedures should be performed in centers specialized in treating these specific conditions.
evidence.explanation: De Maria et al. (2017), PMID:28690482: author recommendation based on experience with these very rare disorders.

evidence.snippet: A multidisciplinary approach by a team experienced in craniofacial anomalies, and an individualized treatment plan are essential for timing and optimizing functional and aesthetic outcome.
evidence.explanation: De Maria et al. (2016), PMID:27196381: individualized management by a team experienced in craniofacial anomalies.

evidence.snippet: we gathered questionnaires from 10 BSS individuals and 2 AMS individuals
evidence.explanation: De Maria et al. (2017), PMID:28690482: composition of the questionnaire sample; pooled findings are not AMS-specific proportions.

treatments/4.description: Coordinate ophthalmic, surgical, audiologic, developmental, dental and genetic care with psychological support. The patient-perspective study emphasizes family and peer acceptance, early age-appropriate discussion of visible differences, and attention to self-esteem as well as physical treatment. Its questionnaire sample included ten people with Barber-Say syndrome and two with AMS; pooled social and surgical outcomes should not be presented as AMS-specific rates. Specialist centers and exchange of surgical experience are recommended by the authors.

evidence.snippet: Additionally, the child shows more prominent features of the disorder when compared to her father documenting variable expression and possible anticipation.
evidence.explanation: A mildly affected transmitting parent, the case parental testing is meant to detect.

evidence.snippet: Mosaic expression of TWIST2 variants is correlated with a less severe phenotype than that reported for the typical expression of TWIST2 variants associated with BSS or AMS.
evidence.explanation: A mosaic parent may be only mildly affected.

evidence.snippet: The recurrence risk for a child of a non-mosaic affected person will likely be 50%
evidence.explanation: De Maria et al. (2017), PMID:28690482, Table 1: autosomal dominant transmission counseling. The paper notes uncertainty about live-born recurrence and provides no quantified risk for mosaic individuals.

treatments/5.description: Counselling after TWIST2 testing of the proband and both parents. Most cases are de novo, but a parent can be mildly affected or mosaic, so an apparently unaffected parent does not exclude recurrence. As for any autosomal dominant disorder, the risk to a child of a non-mosaic affected adult is 50 percent.

evidence.snippet: Treatment of the stenosis by means of temporary tracheostomy and corticosteroids therapy resulted in airway patency restoration and patient's return to her normal activities.
evidence.explanation: Single adult case with confirmed TWIST2 c.223G>A; not evidence for corticosteroid treatment of the inherited malformations.

treatments/6.description: Temporary tracheostomy, ventilation and corticosteroids restored spontaneous breathing in the reported adult with severe airway stenosis and mucosal inflammation. Residual narrowing remained on follow-up. This is a single complication-specific intervention, and the relationship of the stenosis to AMS itself was uncertain.

evidence.snippet: The genetic analysis favors a predominantly dominant-negative mechanism for the action of amino acid substitutions at this highly conserved glutamic acid residue
evidence.explanation: Conclusion of the C. elegans allelic series, which included p.Glu75Lys engineered at the equivalent hlh-8 residue.

evidence.snippet: The resemblance between the three syndromes is considerable, and likely differences seem larger than they actually are due to insufficiently complete evaluation for all characteristics of the three entities in the past.
evidence.explanation: Clinical overlap between AMS, Barber-Say and the loss-of-function disorder Setleis syndrome. INDIRECT: resemblance to a loss-of-function phenotype is consistent with, not proof of, a dominant-negative effect.

evidence.snippet: Heterozygous localized TWIST1 and TWIST2 basic domain substitutions exert antimorphic effects to cause Sweeney-Cox syndrome, Barber-Say syndrome, and ablepharon-macrostomia syndrome, respectively.
evidence.explanation: A later TWIST1 case report restates the Glu75 alleles as antimorphic, summarising the earlier functional work rather than adding new data.

evidence.snippet: The results from these two target genes in heterozygous mutants indicate that Glu29Gln, Glu29Ala, and Glu29Lys are the most likely to represent dominantWnegative proteins that interfere with the ability of WT HLHW8 to promote transcription of egl-15.
evidence.explanation: Kim et al. (2017), PMID:28369379: author interpretation of heterozygous reporter experiments. The accepted-manuscript PDF extracts hyphens as W in these words.

hypotheses/0.description: Mutant TWIST2 is proposed to sequester wild-type TWIST2 or other bHLH partners in transcriptionally ineffective complexes. Residual DNA binding is possible, so this model does not require complete loss of promoter occupancy. In C. elegans, the AMS-equivalent Glu29Lys heterozygote perturbs egg laying and target-gene expression while the heterozygous frameshift-null control resembles wild-type. This favors dominant interference over simple dose reduction in that model. It remains unresolved in human craniofacial and dermal tissues, and is not mutually exclusive with a neomorphic effect.

evidence.snippet: Previous studies have shown that the E75K mutation in twsit2 altered the DNA binding activity of itself, leading to both gain of function and dominant-negative effects.
evidence.explanation: Restates the earlier binding studies of p.Glu75Lys as showing a gain of function alongside the dominant-negative effect. Graded IN_VITRO for the cell-based binding work it summarises.

evidence.snippet: Moreover, a genotype-phenotype correlation was observed, because the two syndromes differed based solely upon the nature of the substituting amino acid: a lysine at TWIST2 residue 75 resulted in AMS, whereas a glutamine or alanine yielded BSS.
evidence.explanation: Different substitutions at one residue give different syndromes, which a residue-specific change in target binding would explain. INDIRECT because the correlation does not itself show new binding.

evidence.snippet: A signiﬁcant number of binding peaks detected for the mutant TWIST2 proteins were not detected for the wild-type protein
evidence.explanation: Marchegiani et al. (2015), PMID:26119818: direct binding evidence underlying the neomorphic hypothesis; disease mediation remains proposed.

evidence.snippet: This observation suggests that besides the dominant negative nature of most of these hlh-8 alleles, some may be acting as neomorphic alleles and interfering with genetic pathways normally not associated with HLHW8 regulation.
evidence.explanation: Kim et al. (2017), PMID:28369379: hypothesis arising from the unusual Glu29Lys sex-myoblast proliferation phenotype. A specific partner or human target was not established.

hypotheses/1.description: Mutant TWIST2 may alter transcription by binding sites that wild-type protein does not occupy. Mutant-only ChIP-seq peaks directly support altered genomic occupancy in HeLa cells. Whether those new targets drive the tissue-specific phenotype, rather than loss of normal binding or both effects, remains unresolved. The worm Glu29Lys allele also produces a sex-myoblast proliferation defect more severe than the null, which the authors interpret as possible interference with another bHLH pathway; this does not establish a specific new human target.

evidence.snippet: Scalp hair is sparse in AMS only, but sparse eyebrows and eyelashes occur in both entities, and general hypertrichosis occurs in BSS.
evidence.explanation: The opposite hair phenotypes of the two allelic syndromes.

open_questions/0.rationale: The two allelic syndromes differ most in hair and in eyelid severity, yet no study among the references cited here has examined hair follicles, eyelid mesenchyme or target genes in either. The binding comparison of the alleles was done in HeLa cells. The hair follicle node in this entry is therefore hypothetical, and a residue-specific difference in target binding is the leading but untested explanation.

evidence.snippet: Developmental impairment was present in two-thirds of patients but was usually mild.
evidence.explanation: The higher estimate from a clinically diagnosed series.

evidence.snippet: Both are characterized by abnormalities in ectoderm-derived structures and cause a very unusual morphology of mainly the face in individuals with otherwise normal cognition and normal physical functioning.
evidence.explanation: The later view, from contact with affected individuals, that cognition is normal.

evidence.snippet: Her intellectual and motor development was normal.
evidence.explanation: Normal development in an adult with molecularly confirmed AMS.

open_questions/1.rationale: Older clinically diagnosed series reported delay in about two-thirds of patients. The molecular series documents variable motor and language delays alongside normal development, with two individuals unassessed and one delayed individual having cerebral hemorrhage. Later patient-perspective reports largely describe normal cognition. These are different outcomes and ascertainment frames; sensory impairment and prolonged hospitalization may also affect development. A systematic prospective assessment of genotyped patients is lacking.

evidence.snippet: Notably, Setleis syndrome patients and Twist2 knockout mice have similar facial features, indicating the gene's conserved role in mammalian development.
evidence.explanation: The knockout mouse matches the recessive loss-of-function disorder, not AMS.

open_questions/2.rationale: The functional results for p.Glu75Lys come from overexpressed human protein (zebrafish mRNA injection, tagged protein in HeLa cells), from engineered alleles in the single C. elegans Twist homolog, and from one heterozygous zebrafish twist2 knock-in whose phenotype (jaw and mouth, emaciation) was described qualitatively in a methods paper. None of these organisms has eyelids, hair or mammalian dermis. Twist2 knockout mice model loss of function, which corresponds to Setleis syndrome rather than to this dominant allele. Whether the mechanism is dominant-negative, neomorphic or both cannot be settled until the allele is studied in mammalian mesenchyme. No mammalian knock-in model was found among the references cited here.

evidence.snippet: The patient reported by Kallish et al. ... showed the phenotype of an acrofacial dysostosis, possibly Nager syndrome, and the differences to AMS were too signiﬁcant to allow inclusion.
evidence.explanation: De Maria et al. (2016), PMID:27196381: differential reassessment of the Kallish report.

evidence.snippet: Lastly, the patient reported by Larumbe et al. ... clearly had severe congenital ichthyosis.
evidence.explanation: De Maria et al. (2016), PMID:27196381: the dental/skin case is excluded from AMS.

evidence.snippet: This chromosome imbalance, the less marked eye signs, the pres- ence of supernumerary nipples, cutis laxa, widely spread joint contractures, edema, and marked developmental delay and seiz- ures make it unlikely that this patient should be diagnosed as having AMS.
evidence.explanation: De Maria et al. (2016), PMID:27196381: reasons for excluding the Pellegrino 18q-rearrangement case.

evidence.snippet: The latter two patients ... tested negatively for TWIST2 mutations
evidence.explanation: De Maria et al. (2016), PMID:27196381: negative TWIST2 testing in two excluded cases. The review prints 2011 for Amor/Savarirayan here; the indexed report and bibliography are from 2001.

open_questions/3.rationale: The 2016 critical review excluded the Pellegrino chromosome-18q case (PMID:8834257), the Amor/Savarirayan CNS case (PMID:11746001), the Kallish limb-anomaly case (PMID:22002929), and the Larumbe dental/skin case (PMID:23198177). The authors considered the Kallish phenotype an acrofacial dysostosis, possibly Nager syndrome, and the Larumbe phenotype severe congenital ichthyosis. The Amor/Savarirayan and Kallish cases tested negative for TWIST2 mutations. These exclusions limit the use of older clinically assembled series for phenotype frequencies and prevent transferring case-specific findings or interventions to molecularly defined AMS.

evidence.snippet: Complete remission rate in 33 patients receiving intensive chemotherapy was 33% and median overall survival (OS) was 33 weeks
evidence.explanation: The adult cohort documents profound treatment resistance and poor outcome.

steps/11.description: Adult AMKL cohorts show adverse cytogenetics, frequent chromosome 1q aberrations, and recurrent mutations unlike the pediatric fusion spectrum. These observations are clinically associated with low remission rates and short survival; which lesions are causal for megakaryoblastic differentiation remains unresolved.

evidence.snippet: OTT-MAL expression deregulated transcriptional activity of the canonical Notch signaling pathway transcription factor recombination signal binding protein for immunoglobulin kappa J region (RBPJ) and caused abnormal fetal megakaryopoiesis.
evidence.explanation: The knock-in model directly supports RBPJ/Notch transcriptional dysregulation.

steps/12.description: The t(1;22) fusion joins RBM15 to MRTFA (formerly MKL1). In a knock-in mouse model the fusion deregulates RBPJ-mediated canonical Notch transcription and abnormal fetal megakaryopoiesis; cooperation with activating MPL is required for short-latency model disease.

evidence.snippet: Expression of CBFA2T3-GLIS2 in Drosophila and murine hematopoietic cells induced bone morphogenic protein (BMP) signaling and resulted in a marked increase in the self-renewal capacity of hematopoietic progenitors.
evidence.explanation: Cross-species functional experiments directly support BMP activation and increased progenitor self-renewal.

steps/13.description: The cryptic inv(16)(p13.3q24.3) CBFA2T3::GLIS2 fusion increases BMP signaling and self-renewal in experimental hematopoietic progenitors. Human transcriptomic studies also associate the fusion with Hippo, TGF-beta, and Hedgehog pathway dysregulation, but those associations are not modeled here as individually proven causal edges.

evidence.snippet: The NUP98-KDM5A fusion oncogene was a potent inducer of maturation arrest, sustaining long-term proliferative and progenitor capacities of engineered cells in optimized culture conditions.
evidence.explanation: The engineered human-cell system directly supports maturation arrest and persistent progenitor capacity.

steps/14.description: NUP98::KDM5A is a potent driver of maturation arrest and long-term proliferative/progenitor capacity in engineered human hematopoietic cells. Model systems also show JAK-STAT upregulation and drug sensitivity, but these preclinical dependencies are not established clinical treatments.

evidence.snippet: These mutations prevent synthesis of full-length GATA1, but not synthesis of a shorter variant that is initiated downstream.
evidence.explanation: This directly establishes the protein-level consequence of the GATA1-truncating mutations.

steps/15.description: In the usual Down syndrome-associated sequence, an acquired GATA1 mutation introduces a premature stop in the N-terminal activation domain. Full-length GATA1 is lost while a shorter downstream-initiated GATA1s protein is retained. The trisomy-21 fetal hematopoietic context and GATA1s cooperate to establish the precursor clone.

evidence.snippet: Hematopoietic differentiation of GATA1 STAG2 double-mutant iPSC lines confirmed GATA1s expression and the loss of functional STAG2 protein, leading to enhanced production of immature megakaryocytic population compared to GATA1 mutant alone.
evidence.explanation: Sequential editing shows that STAG2 loss intensifies the immature megakaryocytic state beyond GATA1s alone.

steps/16.description: In gene-targeted trisomy-21/GATA1-mutant iPSCs, STAG2 loss enhanced production of an immature megakaryocytic population relative to GATA1 mutation alone. This is one progression model; it does not establish that STAG2 loss alone converts TAM into overt ML-DS or AMKL in vivo.

evidence.snippet: One subgroup of patients presented with MLL or NUP98 fusion genes leading to up-regulation of the HOX A cluster genes.
evidence.explanation: Patient genomic and expression data support a shared HOXA program in KMT2A/MLL- and NUP98-rearranged disease.

steps/17.description: KMT2A (historically MLL) and NUP98 fusions define distinct pediatric subgroups but converge at the level of HOXA-cluster upregulation. This node models the shared transcriptional program without treating KMT2A as a cooperating lesion of another fusion subgroup.

evidence.snippet: HOXr cases were found to be significantly enriched in activating MPL mutations
evidence.explanation: Human tumors establish enrichment of activating MPL mutations in this subgroup.

evidence.snippet: Activated JAK-STAT signaling as determined by phosphorylated JAK2 and STAT5 was found in HOXr cells containing a MPL mutation
evidence.explanation: Cytokine-withdrawal experiments provide a functional signaling readout for HOXr/MPL cooperation.

evidence.snippet: We detected GATA1 mutations in TMD blasts from every infant examined.

evidence.snippet: Among those solely observed, peripheral blasts and all other TMD symptoms cleared at a median of 36 and 49 days from diagnosis, respectively.

steps/19.description: TAM is a neonatal clonal myeloid proliferation restricted to infants with trisomy 21 and GATA1s. It often resolves spontaneously and is not itself AMKL, but it is the recognized precursor from which a subset of ML-DS cases later emerge.

evidence.snippet: Nine of ten GATA1 mutant cases had amplifications in the DSCR

steps/20.description: A non-DS pediatric subgroup carries somatic GATA1 truncation without constitutional trisomy 21. Most reported cases had acquired amplification of the Down syndrome critical region and a transcriptional profile closely resembling DS-AMKL.

evidence.snippet: The target cells of AMKL and TAM are immature cells close to stem cells which are capable of differentiating into lineage cells such as megakaryocytes, erythrocytes and myeloid cells.

evidence.snippet: Blasts express at least one or more of the platelet glycoproteins: CD41 (glycoprotein llb), CD61 (glycoprotein IIIa), or CD42b (glycoprotein lb)

steps/21.description: AMKL is defined by an acute leukemic blast population with megakaryocytic differentiation. evidence.snippet: Nine of the 11 cases examined immunohistochemically were positive for platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF)(-BB), especially megakaryoblasts and a few fibroblasts.

evidence.snippet: Biopsy specimens of the liver and lymph node were suggestive of a nonhematopoietic malignant condition because of the cohesiveness of the tumor cells, stromal fibrosis, and the prominent sinusoidal and vascular pattern of infiltration.

steps/23.description: Leukemic megakaryoblasts may form cohesive infiltrates in liver, lymph node, and other tissues. This is particularly well documented in infant t(1;22) AMKL and can resemble a nonhematopoietic small-round-cell tumor.

evidence.snippet: Still, 5-year overall survival (89% ± 3% vs 90% ± 4%; Plog-rank = .64), event-free survival (EFS; 87% ± 3% vs 89% ± 4%; Plog-rank = .71), and cumulative incidence of relapse/nonresponse (CIR/NR; 6% ± 3% vs 6% ± 2%; PGray = .03) did not significantly differ

This evidence supports a specific tested regimen, not arbitrary further deintensification, and applies to the ML-DS trial population rather than a morphology-stratified DS-AMKL subset.
