evidence.snippet: revealed in these families a homozygous G-->A substitution in base 58 of exon-2, resulting in the formation of premature stop codons W328X, W326X, and W328X, of the GCNT2A, -B, and -C isoforms, respectively
evidence.explanation: A nonsense variant in a shared exon, which is why it truncates all three isoforms simultaneously and produces both traits.

evidence.snippet: The activity of the IGnT enzyme expressed from the mutant IGnTC*243A gene was significantly reduced when compared with that expressed from the wild-type IGnTC gene.
evidence.explanation: Direct enzyme assay confirming a variant allele reduces catalytic activity, rather than the loss being inferred from the phenotype alone.

steps/0.description: Biallelic GCNT2 variants abolish or greatly reduce I-branching beta-1,6-N-acetylglucosaminyltransferase activity. Reported alleles include nonsense variants in shared exon 2 that truncate all three isoforms at once, frameshifts, and large Alu-mediated deletions removing whole exons. A missense allele in exon 1C has been shown by direct enzyme assay to reduce rather than abolish activity, which is the finer-grained version of the same lesion.

evidence.snippet: i antigens are predominant on fetal red blood cells, whereas adult human red blood cells fully express I antigens with a very low level of i antigens. The conversion of i to I occurs during the first 18 months after birth as a result of the expression of the I-branching enzyme
evidence.explanation: Describes the developmental conversion this node says fails, and its timing.

evidence.snippet: we showed that cataract-affected individuals in both families have the adult i blood group, whereas unaffected individuals have blood group I as the vast majority of the population
evidence.explanation: Co-segregation of the blood group with the cataract within families.

steps/1.description: Without I-branching activity the erythrocyte surface keeps the fetal linear i structure into adult life instead of converting to branched I. This is the serologically detectable adult i blood group, and it is benign: it causes no haemolysis and no clinical consequence on its own. Its value here is as a marker of the enzymatic lesion, which is how the gene was found in the first place.

evidence.snippet: enzyme function assays and expression patterns for the 3 IGnT transcripts in reticulocytes and lens-epithelium cells were analyzed
evidence.explanation: The isoform expression analysis in lens epithelium specifically, which is what grounds the lens as the affected tissue.

evidence.snippet: The results suggest a molecular genetic mechanism that may explain the partial association of the adult i phenotype with congenital cataracts and indicate that a defect in the I locus may lead directly to the development of congenital cataracts.
evidence.explanation: Note the authors' own hedging: "suggest" and "may lead directly". This is why the node is marked PROVISIONAL rather than carrying a definite mechanism.

steps/2.description:
The I antigen is present on lens epithelium as well as on red cells, and loss of branching there is what produces the cataract. The isoform expression data put the lens-relevant transcripts and the erythroid transcript on different exon 1 variants, which is what makes the two consequences separable.
How the loss of a glycan branch actually causes lens opacification is not established. The published work demonstrates that GCNT2 is expressed in lens epithelium and that its loss co-segregates with cataract; it does not demonstrate the intervening step, whether that is altered membrane protein trafficking, osmotic change, or protein aggregation. This node therefore states the association and stops there rather than supplying a mechanism the literature does not.

evidence.snippet: GCNT2-related cataracts is a disorder characterized by bilateral congenital cataracts (CC) of various types (with or without the adult i blood phenotype) and is caused by biallelic variants in GCNT2
evidence.explanation: Characterises the cataract as bilateral, congenital and morphologically variable, and states the with-or-without relationship to the blood group.

steps/3.description: Bilateral congenital cataract, of varying morphology across reported families.

evidence.snippet: The adult i phenotype has been characterized as the presence of a very low level of I antigen but a high quantity of I antigen on red blood cells (RBCs).
evidence.explanation: The serological definition of the trait. Note the quoted sentence contains a typographical error in the source, which reads "I antigen" where "i antigen" is meant; it is quoted verbatim, as an evidence snippet must be.

steps/4.description: Persistence of the fetal linear i antigen on adult red cells with very low I expression. Serologically striking and clinically benign: it is a marker of the enzyme defect rather than a disease manifestation, and is recorded here because it is the trait that led to the gene.

evidence.snippet: Congenital cataracts affect 3-6 per 10,000 live births and represent one of the leading causes of blindness in children.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the visual consequence at the level of congenital cataract in general. It is not specific to GCNT2, and the notes say so.

steps/5.description: Consequent on the cataract. Congenital cataract is among the leading causes of childhood blindness, which is what makes the timing of surgery the whole of the management question here.

evidence.snippet: The deletion is flanked by Alu repeats of the AluS family on both sides and microsatellite genotyping suggested that its occurrence in the two families was the product of recurrent Alu-Alu repeat-mediated nonhomologous recombinations or an old founder effect.
evidence.explanation: The structural mechanism generating a recurrent large deletion at this locus.

evidence.snippet: Because the GCNT2 locus is rich in Short INterspersed Elements (SINE repeats) and thus likely prone to genomic rearrangements, microdeletions or microduplications at this locus might cause a larger than currently anticipated fraction of apparently isolated autosomal-recessive cataracts.
evidence.explanation: The authors' own inference that copy-number variation at this locus is probably under-ascertained, which is the practical reason a sequencing-only workup is insufficient.

evidence.snippet: We report a novel homozygous frameshift mutation c.1163_1166delATCA, p.(Asn388Argfs*20) as the cause of congenital cataract in two affected siblings.
evidence.explanation: A point-variant allele, showing the spectrum is not exclusively structural.

genes/0.notes: Biallelic loss-of-function variants in GCNT2 at 6p24. Two features of the variant spectrum matter clinically. First, a large share of reported alleles are structural: Alu-mediated deletions of 75 to 98 kb removing one or more exons, arising by non-homologous recombination between flanking AluS elements. The same 93 kb deletion was found in two apparently unrelated Pakistani families, by recurrent Alu-Alu recombination or an old founder effect. A sequencing-only workup can therefore return negative on a patient who has a causal GCNT2 allele. Second, which exon is hit determines which traits appear: shared exons 2 and 3 truncate all isoforms, exon 1C alone gives blood group without cataract, and a truncating exon 1B variant has been reported with cataract.

treatments/0.description: Early lens extraction with subsequent refractive correction and amblyopia management. The treatment is the same as for congenital cataract of any cause, is not directed at the glycosylation defect, and the enzyme deficiency itself is untreated.

evidence.snippet: In Japan, 18 individuals of phenotype i, including our case, have been found in ten unrelated families. Seventeen of them had congenital cataract. Cataract was not found in any of the 45 phenotype I members in these families.
evidence.explanation: The Japanese series that established the strong arm of the association: 17 of 18 phenotype i individuals had cataract, and none of the 45 phenotype I family members did.

evidence.snippet: in comparison with the strong association in Japanese patients between congenital cataracts and the i phenotype, the overall incidence of cataracts in white people with the i phenotype (three of ten people have congenital cataracts) is much lower. In addition, the authors studied the blood of 31 white patients with congenital cataracts and found no patients with the i phenotype.
evidence.explanation: The weak arm, in a White cohort: 3 of 10 rather than 17 of 18, and no i phenotype among 31 patients ascertained through cataract. The contrast between these two series is the population difference the isoform model explains.

evidence.snippet: The presented adult i individual possesses wild-type IGnTA and IGnTB genes but a mutant IGnTC gene with a 243T>A nucleotide substitution, which predicts an amino acid alteration of Asn81Lys.
evidence.explanation: The exon 1C arm of the dissociation: blood group affected, cataract absent, other isoforms intact.

evidence.snippet: We report a proband with CC and a truncating variant in exon 1B (NM_001491.3: c.760dup p.H254Pfs*2) found in trans with a 75 kilobase (kb) copy-number deletion encompassing exon 1B and 1C.
evidence.explanation: The exon 1B arm: a truncating variant in the lens-relevant exon in a proband with cataract.

evidence.snippet: previously reported mutations/deletions have either affected all three isoforms (causing blood group and cataract phenotype) or the C isoform only (causing blood group phenotype only)
evidence.explanation: States the isoform-to-phenotype rule as it stood before the exon 1B case completed it.

evidence.snippet: The expression of the I antigen in blood is regulated only by the IGnTC isoform of GCNT2
evidence.explanation: An independent statement of the erythroid half of the partition: the blood group is governed by the C isoform alone.

hypotheses/0.description:
The three GCNT2 transcripts share exons 2 and 3 and differ in exon 1. GCNT2C is the erythroid transcript and sets the blood group; exon 1B-containing transcripts are the lens-relevant ones. Which exon a variant hits therefore predicts which traits appear, and this is what explains the long-standing clinical observation that the i-cataract association is strong in some populations and weak in others.
This is marked CANONICAL rather than EMERGING because it has the strongest kind of support a genotype-phenotype model can have: a matched pair of dissociating observations in opposite directions. An exon 1C missense variant gives adult i without cataract, and an exon 1B truncating variant gives cataract, each in a person. Neither is a single-case fluke read in isolation; together they are a genetic experiment.

open_questions/0.rationale: The gene, the enzyme, the tissue expression and the co-segregation are all established, and the isoform partition explains which patients get cataract. What is missing is the step in between: no study has shown what the loss of a beta-1,6 branch does to the lens. Candidate routes include altered trafficking or stability of lens membrane glycoproteins, osmotic disturbance, and crystallin aggregation, and nothing in the literature currently distinguishes them. The node is marked PROVISIONAL for this reason, and the source paper itself says only that a defect at the locus "may lead directly" to cataract.

evidence.snippet: The prevalence of CP expressed by gestational age was highest in children born before 28 weeks' gestation (111.80 per 1000 live births; 95% CI 69.53-179.78; p<0.0327).
evidence.explanation: The >50-fold higher CP prevalence in extremely preterm infants establishes prematurity as the dominant risk factor.

evidence.snippet: Brain injury in premature infants is of enormous public health importance because of the large number of such infants who survive with serious neurodevelopmental disability, including major cognitive deficits and motor disability.
evidence.explanation: Links premature brain injury to the motor disability that manifests as cerebral palsy.

evidence.snippet: Hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy, also referred as HIE, is a type of brain injury
evidence.explanation: Defines perinatal hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy — the sequela of perinatal asphyxia — as a neonatal brain injury, the etiologic anchor of the HIE → deep-grey-nuclei → dyskinetic CP branch.

evidence.snippet: newborns with hypoxic ischaemic encephalopathy
evidence.explanation: Cochrane review of therapeutic hypothermia for perinatal hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy, confirming it as a defined perinatal insult with long-term neurodevelopmental sequelae.

evidence.snippet: Among full-term infants, a positive association was found between clinical chorioamnionitis and cerebral palsy (RR, 4.7; 95% CI, 1.3-16.2).
evidence.explanation: Meta-analysis quantifying the association between chorioamnionitis and CP in full-term infants.

evidence.snippet: children with hemiplegic cerebral palsy (CP) due to perinatal arterial ischaemic stroke (AIS)
evidence.explanation: Links perinatal arterial ischemic stroke to hemiplegic cerebral palsy.

evidence.snippet: classical kernicterus with athetoid cerebral palsy, impaired upward gaze and deafness
evidence.explanation: Identifies severe neonatal hyperbilirubinemia (kernicterus) as a cause of athetoid cerebral palsy.

evidence.snippet: traditional and evolving definitions ranging from classical kernicterus with athetoid cerebral palsy, impaired upward gaze and deafness
evidence.explanation: Defines classical kernicterus (bilirubin encephalopathy) as producing athetoid (dyskinetic) cerebral palsy with impaired upgaze and deafness.

steps/5.description: Severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia in the neonate allows lipophilic bilirubin to cross the blood-brain barrier and deposit selectively in the globus pallidus, subthalamic nucleus, and other deep grey structures, causing neurotoxic injury that manifests as dyskinetic (choreoathetoid) cerebral palsy, often with auditory neuropathy and gaze abnormalities.

evidence.snippet: CP was thus defined as a non-progressive developmental disorder of movement and/or posture impairing motor function.
evidence.explanation: States the operational non-progressive, movement/posture definition of cerebral palsy.

evidence.snippet: This operational definition thus excluded progressive neurological disorders such as neurodegenerative diseases.
evidence.explanation: Reinforces that CP is defined by a static (non-progressive) lesion, distinguishing it from neurodegeneration.

evidence.snippet: at the workshop, it was agreed that the concept 'cerebral palsy' should be retained
evidence.explanation: International consensus workshop that produced the retained definition and classification of CP.

steps/6.description: Cerebral palsy results from a static (non-progressive) disturbance or lesion of the developing fetal or infant brain. Although the underlying brain lesion is fixed, its clinical expression evolves as the child grows. The injury is heterogeneous in timing and mechanism (antenatal, perinatal, or early postnatal) and defines the motor phenotype.

evidence.snippet: clinical chorioamnionitis was significantly associated with both cerebral palsy (RR, 1.9; 95% CI, 1.4-2.5) and cPVL (RR, 3.0; 95% CI, 2.2-4.0) in preterm infants.
evidence.explanation: Meta-analysis establishing chorioamnionitis (intrauterine inflammation) as a significant risk factor for CP and cystic PVL, supporting the inflammatory pathway.

steps/7.description: Intrauterine infection/inflammation (chorioamnionitis) and the fetal inflammatory response syndrome sensitize the developing brain. Pro-inflammatory cytokines and activated microglia amplify white matter and neuronal injury and are an independent pathway to cerebral palsy, synergizing with hypoxia-ischemia.

evidence.snippet: HIE pathophysiology involves oxidative stress, mitochondrial energy production failure, glutaminergic excitotoxicity, and apoptosis.
evidence.explanation: Review of neonatal HIE pathophysiology confirming energy failure, excitotoxicity, oxidative stress, and apoptosis as the injury cascade.

steps/8.description: In term infants, an acute perinatal hypoxic-ischemic insult causes energy failure, glutamate excitotoxicity, and a delayed phase of oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and apoptotic/necrotic neuronal death. Depending on severity and duration, injury targets the cerebral cortex, watershed white matter, and — in acute profound asphyxia — the deep grey nuclei (basal ganglia and thalamus).

evidence.snippet: This type of brain injury is generally thought to consist primarily of periventricular leukomalacia (PVL), a distinctive form of cerebral white matter injury.
evidence.explanation: Identifies periventricular leukomalacia (white matter injury) as the primary brain injury of prematurity underlying spastic CP.

evidence.snippet: PVL is frequently accompanied by neuronal/axonal disease, affecting the cerebral white matter, thalamus, basal ganglia, cerebral cortex, brain stem, and cerebellum.
evidence.explanation: Describes the encephalopathy of prematurity — PVL plus neuronal/axonal injury — that produces the CP motor phenotype.

steps/9.description: In preterm infants, hypoxia-ischemia and inflammation injure the periventricular white matter (periventricular leukomalacia). Pre-myelinating oligodendrocyte precursor cells are selectively vulnerable to glutamate excitotoxicity, free-radical (oxidative/nitrative) attack, and cytokine injury, producing focal necrosis and diffuse hypomyelination of the white matter tracts carrying descending motor fibers to the legs — the substrate of spastic diplegia.

evidence.snippet: PVL is frequently accompanied by neuronal/axonal disease, affecting the cerebral white matter, thalamus, basal ganglia, cerebral cortex, brain stem, and cerebellum.
evidence.explanation: Documents thalamic and basal ganglia neuronal injury as part of the encephalopathy underlying cerebral palsy.

steps/10.description: Injury to the basal ganglia and thalamus — from acute profound perinatal asphyxia or bilirubin encephalopathy — disrupts motor control circuits and produces the involuntary movements (dystonia, choreoathetosis) of dyskinetic cerebral palsy.

steps/11.description: Damage to the corticospinal (pyramidal) motor pathways is the anatomic lesion underlying spastic cerebral palsy, removing descending motor output and inhibitory control over the spinal motor apparatus.

evidence.snippet: Movement disorder (spasticity, dystonia, choreoathetosis and/or ataxia) onset occurs within the first few years of life as a manifestation of disrupted brain development
evidence.explanation: Identifies spasticity — the cardinal upper motor neuron feature — as an early clinical manifestation of the developing-brain lesion.

steps/12.description: Loss of descending corticospinal control produces the clinical upper motor neuron syndrome: velocity-dependent hypertonia (spasticity), hyperreflexia, and extensor plantar responses. This is the direct clinical substrate of the spastic motor phenotype.

steps/13.description: Chronic spasticity and abnormal muscle tone acting on a growing skeleton lead to progressive secondary musculoskeletal deformities: muscle-tendon contractures, hip subluxation/dislocation, and neuromuscular scoliosis. These are secondary consequences of the fixed brain lesion, not progression of the lesion itself.

edges/0.description: In preterm infants the developing-brain insult manifests predominantly as periventricular white matter injury.

edges/1.description: In term infants an acute hypoxic-ischemic insult produces the encephalopathy underlying CP.

edges/2.description: Intrauterine infection/inflammation is an independent injury pathway contributing to the developing-brain lesion.

edges/3.description: Injury to periventricular white matter damages the descending corticospinal motor fibers carrying descending motor output to the legs.

edges/4.description: Acute profound asphyxia preferentially injures the metabolically active deep grey nuclei, producing the dyskinetic phenotype.

edges/5.description: Pro-inflammatory cytokines and activated microglia sensitize and injure the vulnerable pre-myelinating oligodendrocytes of the periventricular white matter, amplifying cystic PVL.

edges/6.description: Fetal inflammation synergizes with and lowers the threshold for hypoxic-ischemic neuronal injury.

edges/7.description: Bilirubin deposits selectively in the globus pallidus and subthalamic nucleus, injuring the basal ganglia and producing dyskinetic CP.

edges/8.description: Loss of descending corticospinal control disinhibits the spinal motor apparatus, producing the clinical upper motor neuron syndrome.

edges/9.description: Chronic spasticity acting on the growing skeleton drives progressive contractures, hip displacement, and neuromuscular scoliosis.

evidence.snippet: The prevalence of CP expressed by gestational age was highest in children born before 28 weeks' gestation (111.80 per 1000 live births; 95% CI 69.53-179.78; p<0.0327).
evidence.explanation: Reports cerebral palsy prevalence highest in children born before 28 weeks, at 111.80 per 1000 live births, the extreme-prematurity group in which this lesion predominates.

edges/10.description: Prematurity is not a generic risk factor here: the immature periventricular white matter is selectively vulnerable to ischaemia because pre-myelinating oligodendrocytes are at their most sensitive and the vascular watershed sits there. That is why this exposure produces a characteristic lesion rather than diffuse injury.

evidence.snippet: Hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy, also referred as HIE, is a type of brain injury or damage that is caused by a lack of oxygen to the brain during neonatal period.
evidence.explanation: States that the injury is caused by a lack of oxygen to the brain during the neonatal period, which is the causal claim this link makes rather than merely a definition of the entity.

edges/11.description: The exposure and the node are the same event described clinically and pathologically; interruption of oxygen and blood supply around birth is what hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy consists of.

evidence.snippet: Among full-term infants, a positive association was found between clinical chorioamnionitis and cerebral palsy (RR, 4.7; 95% CI, 1.3-16.2).
evidence.explanation: Reports a relative risk of 4.7 for cerebral palsy with clinical chorioamnionitis among full-term infants, an inflammatory rather than ischaemic route.

edges/12.description: Maternal intrauterine infection reaches the fetal brain through a cytokine response rather than direct invasion, which is why the entry models a neuroinflammation node distinct from the ischaemic ones.

evidence.snippet: children with hemiplegic cerebral palsy (CP) due to perinatal arterial ischaemic stroke (AIS)
evidence.explanation: Describes hemiplegic cerebral palsy arising from perinatal arterial ischaemic stroke, a focal fixed lesion.

edges/13.description: A focal arterial infarct produces a fixed, non-progressive lesion, which is the defining feature of cerebral palsy as a category and typically presents as hemiplegia reflecting the territory involved.

evidence.snippet: classical kernicterus with athetoid cerebral palsy, impaired upward gaze and deafness
evidence.explanation: Describes classical kernicterus with athetoid cerebral palsy, impaired upward gaze and deafness, the clinical syndrome this node represents.

edges/14.description: Unconjugated bilirubin crossing the immature blood-brain barrier deposits in the basal ganglia and brainstem nuclei, producing the athetoid syndrome this node names. It is the one cause here that is essentially fully preventable.

evidence.snippet: We found an enrichment of damaging DNMs in CP cases, which became more apparent when focusing the analysis on genes intolerant to LoF variation
evidence.explanation: Whole-exome sequencing of 250 CP trios shows enrichment of damaging de novo mutations, implicating monogenic genetic contributions (e.g., CTNNB1, TUBA1A).

evidence.snippet: Combined SNV and CNV analysis revealed pathogenic and likely pathogenic variants in 22.7% of unselected individuals with CP.
evidence.explanation: Reports the combined SNV-plus-CNV diagnostic yield (22.7%) in an unselected CP cohort, quantifying the genomic burden of pathogenic variants.

genes/0.notes: A growing fraction of cases previously labeled idiopathic cerebral palsy are explained by monogenic variants (frequently de novo), including genes such as CTNNB1. These genetic causes are increasingly identified by exome/genome sequencing and blur the boundary between cerebral palsy and neurodevelopmental disorders; nonetheless, most cerebral palsy remains acquired/multifactorial.

evidence.snippet: Germline loss-of-function variants in CTNNB1 cause neurodevelopmental disorder with spastic diplegia and visual defects (NEDSDV; OMIM 615075) and are the most frequent, recurrent monogenic cause of cerebral palsy (CP).
evidence.explanation: Establishes CTNNB1 as the most frequent recurrent monogenic cause of a CP diagnosis.

genes/1.notes: Germline loss-of-function CTNNB1 variants are the most frequent recurrent monogenic cause of a cerebral palsy diagnosis, typically presenting as spastic diplegia with visual defects (NEDSDV).

evidence.snippet: of these, two (TUBA1AandCTNNB1) met genome-wide significance.
evidence.explanation: Recurrent damaging de novo mutations in TUBA1A (and CTNNB1) reached genome-wide significance in CP trios.

genes/2.notes: Recurrent de novo TUBA1A variants reached genome-wide significance in a whole-exome study of CP trios; TUBA1A encodes a neuronal alpha-tubulin essential for neuronal migration.

treatments/0.description: Rehabilitation to maintain range of motion, strengthen muscles, and optimize functional mobility.

treatments/1.description: Training in activities of daily living and fine motor / adaptive skills.

treatments/2.description: Management of dysarthria, communication, and feeding/swallowing difficulties.

evidence.snippet: Effective medical and surgical interventions include anti-convulsants, bisphosphonates, botulinum toxin, botulinum toxin plus occupational therapy, botulinum toxin plus casting, diazepam, dentistry, hip surveillance, intrathecal baclofen, scoliosis correction, selective dorsal rhizotomy, and umbilical cord blood cell therapy.
evidence.explanation: Systematic-review traffic-light appraisal listing botulinum toxin among effective CP interventions.

treatments/3.description: Intramuscular botulinum toxin type A for focal spasticity and dystonia.

evidence.snippet: Effective medical and surgical interventions include anti-convulsants, bisphosphonates, botulinum toxin, botulinum toxin plus occupational therapy, botulinum toxin plus casting, diazepam, dentistry, hip surveillance, intrathecal baclofen, scoliosis correction, selective dorsal rhizotomy, and umbilical cord blood cell therapy.
evidence.explanation: Systematic-review traffic-light appraisal listing intrathecal baclofen among effective CP interventions.

treatments/4.description: GABA-B receptor agonist for generalized spasticity; delivered orally or via an implanted intrathecal pump for severe spasticity.

evidence.snippet: Effective medical and surgical interventions include anti-convulsants, bisphosphonates, botulinum toxin, botulinum toxin plus occupational therapy, botulinum toxin plus casting, diazepam, dentistry, hip surveillance, intrathecal baclofen, scoliosis correction, selective dorsal rhizotomy, and umbilical cord blood cell therapy.
evidence.explanation: Systematic-review traffic-light appraisal listing selective dorsal rhizotomy among effective CP interventions.

treatments/5.description: Neurosurgical sectioning of selected dorsal (sensory) nerve rootlets to reduce lower-limb spasticity in carefully selected ambulant children with spastic diplegia.

treatments/6.description: Muscle-tendon lengthening, hip reconstruction, and scoliosis correction for established musculoskeletal deformities.

treatments/7.description: Coordinated management including orthoses, assistive devices, nutrition, management of epilepsy, pain, and orthopedic surveillance (e.g., hip surveillance programs).

evidence.snippet: Our meta-analysis including eight RCTs showed that magnesium sulfate reduced the risk of cerebral palsy without a significant change in pediatric mortality.
evidence.explanation: Meta-analysis of RCTs showing antenatal magnesium sulfate reduces CP risk in preterm-labor pregnancies.

evidence.snippet: Effective prevention strategies include antenatal corticosteroids, magnesium sulfate, caffeine, and neonatal hypothermia.
evidence.explanation: Systematic review listing antenatal magnesium sulfate among effective CP prevention strategies.

treatments/8.description: Magnesium sulfate given to women at risk of imminent preterm birth reduces the risk of cerebral palsy in the offspring. This is an established antenatal neuroprotective (preventive) intervention, not a treatment of established CP.

evidence.snippet: There is evidence from the 11 randomised controlled trials included in this systematic review (N = 1505 infants) that therapeutic hypothermia is beneficial in term and late preterm newborns with hypoxic ischaemic encephalopathy.
evidence.explanation: Cochrane meta-analysis showing cooling reduces death and neurodevelopmental disability after neonatal HIE, a major cause of CP.

treatments/9.description: Whole-body or selective head cooling initiated within 6 hours of birth in term/late-preterm newborns with moderate-to-severe hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy reduces death and long-term neurodevelopmental disability, including cerebral palsy. This is a preventive neuroprotective intervention applied in the neonatal period, not a treatment of established CP.

evidence.snippet: For example, XCX mice display gait deficits following hypoxic injury, highlighting the potential for modelling perinatal hypoxia and associated cerebral palsy49 as well as human neurodevelopmental disorders more broadly.
evidence.explanation: The authors explicitly frame perinatal hypoxia and associated cerebral palsy as potential applications, supporting inclusion as a prospective connection.

evidence.snippet: The observed behavioural outputs probably reflect interactions between the human graft and preserved mouse subcortical circuits, but whether graft-derived neurons are necessary or sufficient for specific behaviours remains unclear.
evidence.explanation: The authors leave graft-neuron necessity and sufficiency for behaviour unresolved.

evidence.snippet: At the timepoints examined, the XCX graft lacked several features of mature cortical circuitry, including complete areal patterning, a well-defined laminar cortical plate, full representation of GABAergic interneurons and a mature transcriptional profile.
evidence.explanation: Documents incomplete areal patterning, lamination, interneuron representation and transcriptional maturity.

open_questions/0.rationale: The paper introduces a human cortical development and circuit platform and demonstrates hypoxic injury as an application. Its cerebral-palsy connection is prospective. The demonstrated cellular responses and short-term mouse gait changes do not establish the persistent human motor syndrome, the full hypoxic-ischemic injury cascade, or a causal chain from HIF1α through gliosis to impaired gait. Immature cortical organization, mixed human and mouse cellular contributions, and unresolved graft-specific behavioural causality constrain translation. Longitudinal motor assessment and graft-specific perturbations would be needed to assess that connection.

evidence.snippet: All patients with types A and B NPD have mutations in the gene encoding ASM (SMPD1), and thus the disease is more accurately referred to as ASM deficiency (ASMD).
evidence.explanation: SMPD1 mutation and acid sphingomyelinase deficiency underlie all ASMD forms including the intermediate phenotype.

steps/1.description: Biallelic SMPD1 variants leave intermediate residual acid sphingomyelinase activity, greater than in infantile type A but insufficient for normal sphingomyelin turnover. The residual activity partially protects the CNS, giving an intermediate neurovisceral phenotype rather than the fatal infantile course.

evidence.snippet: varying degrees of lipid storage and foam cell infiltration in tissues
evidence.explanation: Sphingomyelin storage produces foam-cell infiltration of viscera and, in intermediate disease, partial CNS involvement.

steps/2.description: Sphingomyelin accumulates in reticuloendothelial macrophages (spleen, liver, lung, marrow) and, because residual enzyme is insufficient to fully protect neurons, also variably in the nervous system, producing the combined neurovisceral picture of intermediate ASMD.

evidence.snippet: Type B patients also have hepatosplenomegaly and pathologic alterations of their lungs
evidence.explanation: Hepatosplenomegaly characterizes chronic (type B and intermediate) ASMD.

steps/3.description: Splenomegaly is a near-constant feature of chronic ASMD.

evidence.snippet: Type B patients also have hepatosplenomegaly and pathologic alterations of their lungs
evidence.explanation: Hepatosplenomegaly (including hepatomegaly) characterizes chronic ASMD.

steps/4.description: Hepatomegaly accompanies splenomegaly as part of the visceral storage burden.

evidence.snippet: Intermediate patients also have been reported with mild to moderate neurological findings.
evidence.explanation: Intermediate ASMD has mild-to-moderate neurological involvement, unlike type B.

steps/5.description: Later-onset and variable neurological involvement (e.g., developmental delay, ataxia, or slowly progressive deterioration) distinguishes the intermediate form from non-neuronopathic type B.

evidence.snippet: most patients have interstitial lung disease with progressive impairment of pulmonary function
evidence.explanation: Interstitial lung disease is a major feature of chronic ASMD.

steps/6.description: Progressive interstitial lung disease from pulmonary storage macrophages.

edges/1.description: Partial enzyme deficiency drives combined visceral and partial neuronal storage.

evidence.snippet: Type B patients also have hepatosplenomegaly and pathologic alterations of their lungs
evidence.explanation: Hepatosplenomegaly includes splenic enlargement in chronic ASMD.

edges/2.description: Reticuloendothelial sphingomyelin storage and foam-cell infiltration enlarge the spleen as part of chronic neurovisceral ASMD.

evidence.snippet: Type B patients also have hepatosplenomegaly and pathologic alterations of their lungs
evidence.explanation: Hepatosplenomegaly includes hepatic enlargement in chronic ASMD.

edges/3.description: Hepatic reticuloendothelial sphingomyelin storage and foam-cell infiltration enlarge the liver as part of chronic neurovisceral ASMD.

evidence.snippet: Some patients with ASMD who survive beyond early childhood have intermediate phenotypes (variant NPD B) characterized by combinations of non-neurologic and mild to severe neurologic symptoms.
evidence.explanation: This links the intermediate ASMD phenotype to neurologic symptoms alongside non-neurologic storage manifestations.

edges/4.description: Intermediate residual enzyme activity can leave nervous-system involvement alongside non-neurologic storage disease.

evidence.snippet: most patients have interstitial lung disease with progressive impairment of pulmonary function
evidence.explanation: This supports interstitial lung disease as a pulmonary manifestation of chronic ASMD.

edges/5.description: Pulmonary sphingomyelin storage and inflammatory-cell infiltration contribute to chronic interstitial lung disease in ASMD.

evidence.snippet: Acid sphingomyelinase deficiency (ASMD), a rare lysosomal storage disease, is an autosomal recessive genetic disorder caused by different SMPD1 mutations.
evidence.explanation: SMPD1 mutations cause ASMD; intermediate residual activity yields the chronic neurovisceral phenotype.

evidence.explanation: Olipudase alfa is the approved ERT for the visceral disease of ASMD.

evidence.explanation: Progressive multisystem complications require supportive management.

evidence.snippet: This genetic alteration leads to abnormal intracellular accumulation as well as urinary excretion of
evidence.explanation: NEU1 deficiency causes intracellular accumulation and urinary excretion of sialyloligosaccharides.

evidence.explanation: Hydrops fetalis/neonatal ascites defines the most acute congenital form of sialidosis type II.

steps/3.description: Nonimmune hydrops fetalis or neonatal ascites is the defining presentation of the congenital form, from severe prenatal storage.

steps/4.description: Coarse/dysmorphic facies of the severe (type II) form.

evidence.explanation: Hepatosplenomegaly is present at birth in congenital sialidosis type II.

edges/1.description: Loss of sialidase prevents desialylation, so sialylated substrates accumulate from before birth.

severity of clinical presentation of sialidosis.

treatments/0.description: No curative therapy exists; the congenital form is often fatal perinatally and management is supportive and palliative.

evidence.snippet: Siblings in Family 1 were compound heterozygous for the c.5135C>T (p.Ala1712Val) missense substitution and the c.4478C>G (p.Ser1493*) nonsense substitution; in Family 2 were homozygous for the c.4478C>A (p.Ser1493*) nonsense substitution and in Family 3 were homozygous for the c.7518-1G>A (p.Trp2507Argfs*4) substitution.
evidence.explanation: Lists the causal biallelic genotypes across the three founding families.

evidence.snippet: Expression analysis in patient-derived skin fibroblasts demonstrated absence of the DMXL2 protein, revealing a loss of function phenotype.
evidence.explanation: Shows the alleles are functionally null at the protein level in patient cells, which is why this node is modelled as complete loss of function.

steps/1.description: Biallelic DMXL2 variants - nonsense, splice-site and missense alleles - are the initiating lesion, and they behave as a null: patient fibroblasts contain no detectable DMXL2 protein. This node captures the single concept of the genetic lesion.

evidence.snippet: mRAVE consists of DMXL1 or DMXL2, WDR7 and the central linker ROGDI.
evidence.explanation: Identifies DMXL2 as an alternative core subunit of the metazoan RAVE complex, the assembly factor this node is about.

evidence.snippet: mRAVE then catalyzes V1-VO assembly, enabling lysosomal acidification, neurotransmitter loading into vesicles and ATG16L1 recruitment for LC3/ATG8 conjugation onto single membranes.
evidence.explanation: States the three downstream functions that depend on mRAVE-catalysed assembly, which are the three branches taken from this node.

evidence.snippet: DMXL2 is highly expressed in the brain and at synaptic terminals, regulates v-ATPase assembly and activity and participates in intracellular signalling pathways
evidence.explanation: The founding report's own statement of DMXL2's function; evidence source is OTHER because this sentence is the paper's background summary of prior work, not a result of the study.

evidence.snippet: DMXL2 expression is highly enriched in brain, although it is also expressed in other tissues.
evidence.explanation: Explains why loss of the DMXL2 paralogue produces a brain-predominant phenotype while the ubiquitous DMXL1 paralogue continues to serve other tissues. Evidence source is OTHER because this is a review.

evidence.snippet: The DMXL2 gene encodes for rabconnectin-3α, a member of the WD40 repeat (WDR) protein family that is highly expressed in the brain.
evidence.explanation: Independent statement of the gene product's identity and its brain enrichment. Evidence source is OTHER because this is a review.

steps/2.description: DMXL2 (rabconnectin-3alpha) is one of the two alternative large subunits of the metazoan RAVE complex, which also contains WDR7 and the linker ROGDI. mRAVE catalyses the joining of the cytosolic V1 and membrane-embedded VO halves of the vacuolar H+-ATPase after the proton gradient has been dissipated. Without it, the pump cannot be reassembled on demand, and every membrane compartment that depends on regulated V-ATPase assembly loses its acidification capacity. DMXL2 is the brain-enriched paralogue, which is why loss is tolerated elsewhere and not in neurons.

evidence.snippet: Patients' fibroblasts also exhibited an increased LysoTracker® signal associated with decreased endolysosomal markers and degradative processes.
evidence.explanation: Direct measurement of endolysosomal dysfunction in cells from affected individuals.

steps/3.description: Patient fibroblasts show a disturbed endolysosomal compartment: an increased LysoTracker signal alongside reduced endolysosomal markers and reduced degradative capacity. This node captures the single concept of a dysfunctional, incorrectly acidified endolysosomal system.

evidence.snippet: Defective endolysosomal homeostasis was accompanied by impaired autophagy, revealed by lower LC3II signal, accumulation of polyubiquitinated proteins, and autophagy receptor p62, with morphological alterations of the autolysosomal structures on electron microscopy.
evidence.explanation: Multi-assay demonstration of a block in autophagic flux in patient cells.

steps/4.description: Autophagic flux is blocked: LC3-II falls, polyubiquitinated proteins and the autophagy receptor p62 accumulate, and autolysosomal structures are morphologically abnormal on electron microscopy. This node captures the single concept of failed autophagic degradation.

evidence.snippet: In neurons, the V-ATPase is required to package certain neurotransmitters into synaptic vesicles
evidence.explanation: States the dependence of vesicular neurotransmitter packaging on the V-ATPase. Evidence source is OTHER because this sentence is the paper's introductory background rather than its own experiment, and directness is INDIRECT because it is about the pump, not about DMXL2 loss.

evidence.snippet: Rabconnectin-3α interacts with the synaptic vesicle (SV)-associated G-protein Rab3A at the synapse and is strictly involved in the assembly and incorporation of v-ATPase into SVs through its Rav1p domain, homologous to the yeast v-ATPase regulator Rav1p
evidence.explanation: Connects DMXL2 specifically to getting the V-ATPase onto synaptic vesicles, which is what makes this node a DMXL2 consequence rather than a general statement about the pump. Evidence source is OTHER because this is a review; one of its authors co-authored the founding DEE81 report.

steps/5.description: Loading of neurotransmitter into a synaptic vesicle is driven by the proton gradient the vesicular V-ATPase generates. Where the pump cannot be assembled, vesicles are not filled. This node captures the single concept of a presynaptic vesicle-filling failure and is the entry point of the synaptic-vesicle hypothesis for the epilepsy.

evidence.snippet: Altered lysosomal homeostasis and defective autophagy were recapitulated in Dmxl2-silenced mouse hippocampal neurons, which exhibited impaired neurite elongation and synaptic loss.
evidence.explanation: Reproduces the cellular defect in neurons and adds the neurite and synapse phenotype. Evidence source is IN_VITRO because this is a cultured primary neuron preparation, not a whole animal.

steps/6.description: Neurons in which Dmxl2 is silenced show the same lysosomal and autophagic abnormalities as patient fibroblasts, and in addition fail to elongate their neurites and lose synapses. This node captures the single concept of a neuron-intrinsic failure to build normal processes and connections.

evidence.snippet: Ohtahara syndrome, early infantile epileptic encephalopathy with a suppression burst EEG pattern, is an aetiologically heterogeneous condition starting in the first weeks or months of life with intractable seizures and profound developmental disability.
evidence.explanation: Defines the electroclinical syndrome these patients were shown to have; the suppression-burst pattern is the network-level signature of hypersynchronous discharge. Evidence source is OTHER and directness INDIRECT because this sentence defines Ohtahara syndrome generally rather than reporting a DEE81 measurement.

steps/7.description: Populations of neurons fire excessively and synchronously. In DEE81 the signature is electrographic: the founding cohort's phenotype was Ohtahara syndrome, defined by a suppression-burst EEG in which high-amplitude synchronous bursts alternate with near-flat suppression, from the first weeks of life. This node captures the single concept of network hyperexcitability and conforms to the shared epilepsy final common pathway.

evidence.snippet: Early brain MRI investigations in the first months of life revealed thin corpus callosum with brain hypomyelination in all.
evidence.explanation: Structural evidence, present from the earliest imaging, that brain development was already abnormal before birth.

evidence.snippet: These clinical findings are consistent with a developmental brain disorder that begins in the prenatal brain, prevents neural connections from reaching the expected stages at birth, and follows a progressive course.
evidence.explanation: The authors' reading of the combined imaging and clinical data as a prenatal-onset developmental disorder with a progressive course.

steps/8.description: Connectivity fails to reach the expected stage by birth. Imaging in the first months of life already shows a thin corpus callosum and brain hypomyelination in every patient, which is a prenatal rather than a postnatal deficit. This node captures the single concept of an antenatally established structural brain deficit.

evidence.snippet: Follow-up MRI scans in three patients revealed progressive moderate brain shrinkage with leukoencephalopathy.
evidence.explanation: Serial imaging in three of the six patients documents progressive volume loss with white-matter change.

steps/9.description: Serial imaging shows the brain losing volume, with white-matter disease, over follow-up - a degenerative course superimposed on the developmental deficit. This node captures the single concept of progressive structural brain loss and is what distinguishes DEE81 from a static encephalopathy.

evidence.snippet: The severe developmental and epileptic encephalopathy manifested from the first day of life and was associated with deafness, mild peripheral polyneuropathy and dysmorphic features.
evidence.explanation: Dates onset to the first day of life and names the accompanying syndromic features.

evidence.snippet: Despite initial treatment with multiple antiepileptics, seizures persisted, prompting a thorough diagnostic evaluation.
evidence.explanation: Documents drug resistance in an independently reported DEE81 neonate.

steps/10.description: The clinical endpoint of the epileptic arm: recurrent seizures beginning in the first day or days of life that do not respond to antiseizure medication. This node captures the single concept of the drug-resistant seizure state and conforms to the shared epilepsy final common pathway.

evidence.snippet: Five patients died within the first 9 years of life and none achieved developmental, communicative or motor skills following birth.
evidence.explanation: Records the absence of any developmental attainment across the founding cohort.

steps/11.description: Profound, non-progressing-forward developmental impairment: patients acquired no developmental, communicative or motor skill after birth. Both the antenatal connectivity deficit and the neonatal-onset epilepsy converge here. This node captures the single concept of the developmental half of the syndrome.

evidence.snippet: The severe developmental and epileptic encephalopathy manifested from the first day of life and was associated with deafness, mild peripheral polyneuropathy and dysmorphic features.
evidence.explanation: States the epileptic encephalopathy and its first-day-of-life onset.

steps/12.description: The defining electroclinical picture: intractable seizures from the first day of life with profound developmental impairment, presenting as Ohtahara syndrome.

evidence.snippet: Here, we report the case of a neonate born from a consanguineous marriage, presenting with refractory focal seizures shortly after birth.
evidence.explanation: An independently reported DEE81 patient with refractory seizures from shortly after birth.

evidence.snippet: The severe developmental and epileptic encephalopathy manifested from the first day of life and was associated with deafness, mild peripheral polyneuropathy and dysmorphic features.
evidence.explanation: Covers the six patients of the founding cohort, all of whom had the epileptic encephalopathy from the first day of life.

steps/13.description: Seizures are universal and refractory. The founding cohort presented as Ohtahara syndrome; the one later-reported neonate had refractory focal seizures.

evidence.snippet: Here, we report the case of a neonate born from a consanguineous marriage, presenting with refractory focal seizures shortly after birth.
evidence.explanation: Names the seizure onset as focal in this patient.

steps/14.description: Focal-onset seizures were the presenting semiology in the one DEE81 patient reported outside the founding cohort.

evidence.snippet: Ohtahara syndrome, early infantile epileptic encephalopathy with a suppression burst EEG pattern, is an aetiologically heterogeneous condition starting in the first weeks or months of life with intractable seizures and profound developmental disability.
evidence.explanation: Defines suppression-burst as the EEG pattern of Ohtahara syndrome, which is the diagnosis these patients were given. Directness is INDIRECT and the source is OTHER because this sentence defines the syndrome rather than reporting these patients' recordings.

steps/15.description: Suppression-burst is the EEG signature of Ohtahara syndrome, the electroclinical diagnosis carried by every patient of the founding cohort.

evidence.snippet: Five patients died within the first 9 years of life and none achieved developmental, communicative or motor skills following birth.
evidence.explanation: Absence of any skill acquisition in all six patients is the profound end of the developmental-delay scale.

steps/16.description: No developmental, communicative or motor skill was acquired after birth in any patient of the founding cohort.

evidence.snippet: Early brain MRI investigations in the first months of life revealed thin corpus callosum with brain hypomyelination in all.
evidence.explanation: Reports a thin corpus callosum in all patients on early imaging.

steps/17.description: A thin corpus callosum was present on the earliest MRI in every patient.

evidence.snippet: Early brain MRI investigations in the first months of life revealed thin corpus callosum with brain hypomyelination in all.
evidence.explanation: Reports brain hypomyelination in all patients on early imaging.

steps/18.description: Brain hypomyelination was present on the earliest MRI in every patient.

evidence.snippet: Follow-up MRI scans in three patients revealed progressive moderate brain shrinkage with leukoencephalopathy.
evidence.explanation: Documents progressive brain volume loss on serial imaging.

steps/19.description: Follow-up imaging shows progressive brain shrinkage, in three of the six patients in whom serial scans were available.

evidence.snippet: Follow-up MRI scans in three patients revealed progressive moderate brain shrinkage with leukoencephalopathy.
evidence.explanation: Reports leukoencephalopathy on follow-up imaging.

steps/20.description: White-matter disease appears alongside the progressive volume loss on follow-up imaging.

edges/1.description: Absence of DMXL2 protein removes the rabconnectin-3alpha subunit of the metazoan RAVE complex that assembles the V-ATPase.

edges/2.description: Without on-demand V1-VO assembly, endosomes and lysosomes cannot maintain their acidic lumen.

edges/3.description: Vesicular neurotransmitter transporters run on the proton-motive force the V-ATPase generates, so failure to assemble the pump on synaptic vesicles leaves them unfilled.

edges/4.description: Autophagic flux terminates in the lysosome, so a compartment that cannot degrade its contents blocks the pathway at its final step.

edges/5.description: Silencing Dmxl2 in cultured neurons reproduces the lysosomal and autophagic defect and costs those neurons neurite length and synapses.

edges/6.description: A sustained block in autophagic degradation is the plausible route to the progressive tissue loss seen on serial imaging, but no study has connected the two directly in this disease, so the intermediates are unstated.

evidence.snippet: which could suggest that loss of synaptic vesicle function is the basis of the aberrant neurological activity associated with DMXL2 deficiency
evidence.explanation: The source states this as a suggestion, which is why the edge is indirect with unknown intermediates and is assigned to a hypothesis group rather than asserted. Evidence source is OTHER because this is a review.

edges/7.description: Proposed, not demonstrated: if synaptic vesicles cannot be filled, synaptic transmission fails and network activity becomes abnormal. No electrophysiological measurement has been made in a DEE81 neuron, so the intermediates between vesicle-filling failure and hypersynchrony are unknown.

edges/8.description: Neurons that cannot extend processes or form synapses cannot build normal connectivity in the developing brain.

edges/9.description: Proposed, not demonstrated: abnormally wired networks with reduced synaptic density are the route to hypersynchronous discharge on this hypothesis. No excitability measurement has been reported in this model or in patient neurons.

edges/10.description: An antenatally established connectivity deficit is the developmental half of the developmental and epileptic encephalopathy.

edges/11.description: The same brains that start hypomyelinated go on to shrink, but nothing published establishes whether the progressive loss is a continuation of the developmental lesion or a separate degenerative process.

edges/12.description: A commissure that failed to form normally is the imaging correlate of the antenatal connectivity deficit.

edges/13.description: Deficient myelination on the earliest scans is the other imaging correlate of the same antenatal deficit.

edges/14.description: Hypersynchronous network discharge is expressed clinically as seizures.

edges/15.description: Bursts of synchronous high-amplitude activity alternating with near-flat suppression are the electrographic expression of this network state.

edges/16.description: This node is the mechanism-side statement of the clinical seizure phenotype.

edges/17.description: Focal onset is the semiology recorded in the one patient described outside the founding cohort.

edges/18.description: Refractory seizures from the first day of life, together with the developmental impairment, constitute the epileptic encephalopathy.

edges/19.description: Continuous early-life epileptic activity is conventionally held to worsen development, and it is the epileptic half of the name, but in DEE81 the developmental deficit is already present at birth and no study separates the seizure-driven contribution from the antenatal one.

edges/20.description: The clinical measure of this node is the complete absence of developmental attainment.

edges/21.description: Progressive volume loss is reported on serial MRI as brain shrinkage.

edges/22.description: White-matter disease accompanies the volume loss on the same scans.

evidence.snippet: Siblings in Family 1 were compound heterozygous for the c.5135C>T (p.Ala1712Val) missense substitution and the c.4478C>G (p.Ser1493*) nonsense substitution; in Family 2 were homozygous for the c.4478C>A (p.Ser1493*) nonsense substitution and in Family 3 were homozygous for the c.7518-1G>A (p.Trp2507Argfs*4) substitution.
evidence.explanation: The causal genotypes reported across the three founding families.

evidence.snippet: DMXL2 (Rabconnectin-3α) and WDR7 (Rabconnectin-3β) together comprise a synaptic Rabconnectin-3 complex in an apparent 1:1 ratio (Kawabe et al., 2003).
evidence.explanation: Identifies the gene product as rabconnectin-3alpha and its obligate partner. Evidence source is OTHER because this is a review.

evidence.snippet: Despite initial treatment with multiple antiepileptics, seizures persisted, prompting a thorough diagnostic evaluation.
evidence.explanation: Documents that multiple antiseizure medications were given and did not control the seizures.

treatments/0.description: Multiple antiseizure medications were used in the one DEE81 patient whose treatment course is described, and seizures persisted. No disease-modifying therapy exists, and no antiseizure agent has been reported to control seizures in this disorder.

hypotheses/0.description: DMXL2 is enriched in brain and at synaptic terminals, and the V-ATPases that acidify synaptic vesicles - and so drive neurotransmitter loading - depend on rabconnectin-3alpha for assembly. On this model the epilepsy is a synaptic transmission failure, and the lysosomal and autophagic abnormalities are a parallel consequence of the same assembly defect rather than the route to the seizures. It is EMERGING rather than canonical because the proposal is explicitly framed as a suggestion in the source review, and no electrophysiological measurement has been made in a DEE81 neuron.

hypotheses/1.description: On this model the proximate lesion is the endolysosomal and autophagic block that is directly demonstrated in patient fibroblasts, and the epilepsy follows from the resulting failure of neurite elongation and synapse formation, which was reproduced in Dmxl2-silenced mouse hippocampal neurons. This is the arm with the most direct experimental support in patient material, but the step from impaired neurite and synapse development to hypersynchronous discharge has not been measured.

evidence.snippet: Complete loss of Dmxl2 is lethal at the embryonic stage in mice
evidence.explanation: Establishes that the genotype-matched whole-animal model cannot be made by simple knockout.

open_questions/0.rationale: Complete loss of Dmxl2 is embryonic lethal in mice, so no whole-organism model of the recessive human genotype exists; the viable heterozygote has the wrong zygosity and a phenotype (macrocephaly) the patients do not have. The two systems that do carry the human lesion - patient fibroblasts and Dmxl2-silenced neurons - are both cultures, and neither can produce a seizure, an EEG, myelin, or a progressive atrophy. That is why the edges from the cellular defects to network hyperexcitability are marked INDIRECT_UNKNOWN_INTERMEDIATES: the gap is not that nobody has looked, it is that the systems available cannot look.

evidence.snippet: We also found that DMXL2 harbors a homozygous truncating variant
evidence.explanation: The primary report of the additional homozygous DMXL2 patient at issue.

evidence.snippet: although the associated phenotypes are sufficiently different from the original reports that they represent phenotypic expansion or potentially distinct allelic disorders
evidence.explanation: The reporting group's own classification of this class of finding, which is what makes the assignment genuinely open rather than settled.

evidence.snippet: An additional homozygous variant in DMXL2 has been reported in a patient with consanguineous parents and presenting DEE and macrocephaly
evidence.explanation: The later review counts the same patient as a DMXL2 DEE case, which is the competing reading. Evidence source is OTHER because this is a review.

open_questions/1.rationale: A homozygous DMXL2 truncating variant was reported in a child with intellectual disability, epilepsy, macrocephaly and dysmorphism. The reporting group classified it as a phenotype different enough from the published DMXL2 associations to represent a phenotypic expansion or a potentially distinct allelic disorder, and contrasted it explicitly with the endocrine phenotype. A later review counts the same patient as an additional DMXL2 developmental and epileptic encephalopathy case. Both readings are defensible from the published text and they give different answers to how many DEE81 patients exist, which is why the prevalence record here counts only the seven patients described as this disease. Resolving it needs the residual-function question answered: the polyendocrine phenotype is reported with a variant retaining partial transcript, and whether this child's truncating allele leaves residual protein has not been measured.

open_questions/2.rationale: Both routes are supported at the level of cell biology and neither has been tested against network excitability. The published patient-cell work establishes the lysosomal and autophagic block; the synaptic-vesicle route is stated as a suggestion in a review. No electrophysiological recording has been reported from a DEE81 neuron or from a Dmxl2-deficient network, so the step from either cellular defect to hypersynchronous discharge is unmeasured. This matters therapeutically: the two routes imply different intervention points.

evidence.snippet: Mutations in DMXL2 have been connected to Ohtahara Syndrome, nonsyndromic hearing loss, and neuroendocrine dysfunction (Tata et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2017; Esposito et al., 2019).
evidence.explanation: Establishes that DMXL2 carries three distinct disease associations, which is the premise of this gap. Evidence source is OTHER because this is a review.

open_questions/3.rationale: Distinguishing these entities is a practical curation and diagnostic problem, not only a mechanistic one: a gene-level literature or variant search on DMXL2 returns all three, and their evidence must not be mixed. Zygosity is the obvious axis - DEE81 and the polyendocrine syndrome are biallelic while DFNA71 is heterozygous - but nothing published explains why one biallelic loss-of-function genotype produces a neonatal encephalopathy and another produces an endocrine and peripheral-nerve phenotype, and no allelic series with matched functional measurements exists. Note also that heterozygous DMXL2 deletions occur incidentally in aromatase excess syndrome, where the causal lesion is a neighbouring CYP19A1 rearrangement; those carriers are not reported to have any DMXL2-attributable phenotype.

evidence.snippet: Rare heterozygous variants in exons 33-34 of the SRCAP gene are associated with Floating-Harbor syndrome and have a dominant-negative mechanism of action. At variance, heterozygous null alleles falling in other parts of the same gene cause developmental delay, hypotonia, musculoskeletal defects, and behavioral abnormalities (DEHMBA) syndrome.
evidence.explanation: States the allelic rule this node encodes - null allele outside the hotspot for DEHMBA, dominant-negative inside it for FLHS - in one sentence.

evidence.snippet: Truncating variants in exons 33 and 34 of the SNF2-related CREBBP activator protein (SRCAP) gene cause the neurodevelopmental disorder (NDD) Floating-Harbor syndrome (FLHS), characterized by short stature, speech delay, and facial dysmorphism.
evidence.explanation: Fixes the hotspot coordinates that outside is defined against, and the FLHS phenotype this disease is being separated from.

evidence.snippet: RNA sequencing and qRT-PCR confirmed significant depletion of SRCAP expression and low-level exon skipping in the proband.
evidence.explanation: Direct measurement that a non-hotspot lesion reduces SRCAP transcript, which is the loss-of-function claim this node makes rather than a prediction from variant class.

steps/1.description:
A de novo heterozygous variant in SRCAP that destroys the allele - nonsense, frameshift, canonical or deep-intronic splice-altering, or a retrotransposon insertion - and lies proximal or distal to exons 33-34.
The location is the whole point. A truncation inside exons 33-34 escapes nonsense-mediated decay and yields a stable shortened protein, which is Floating-Harbor syndrome; anywhere else the transcript is degraded and the cell is simply short of SRCAP. So a curator or laboratory reading a novel SRCAP truncation should ask where it sits before predicting which disease it causes, and should not treat DEHMBA as a milder or severer FLHS.

evidence.snippet: The main function of the SRCAP complex is to promote the exchange of histone H2A with the H2A.Z variant.
evidence.explanation: The complex's catalytic function, which is what a dosage shortfall here reduces. Graded OTHER because this is the paper's statement of established biochemistry rather than a result it reports.

steps/2.description: Reduced SRCAP dosage leaves the SRCAP chromatin-remodelling complex - the human counterpart of yeast SWR1 - operating below its normal capacity. The complex's defining job is ATP-dependent exchange of canonical H2A for the histone variant H2A.Z, so a shortfall here is a shortfall in H2A.Z deposition rather than a general chromatin defect.

evidence.snippet: The chromatin remodeler SRCAP plays a critical role in depositing the histone variant H2A.Z, which is essential for transcriptional regulation, chromatin accessibility, and neurodevelopmental processes.
evidence.explanation: Names the deposition function and the reason its failure is transcriptional.

steps/3.description: H2A.Z is under-deposited at the complex's target nucleosomes, concentrated at activity-dependent and neurodevelopmental genes rather than distributed at random. Because H2A.Z occupancy sets chromatin accessibility, this is the step where a protein-dosage problem becomes a transcriptional one.

evidence.snippet: Comparing proximal variants with typically developing controls, we identified a DNAm signature distinct from the FLHS signature.
evidence.explanation: The signature itself, and its separation from the FLHS signature.

evidence.snippet: A machine-learning model, based on the FLHS DNAm signature, negatively classified all our tested subjects.
evidence.explanation: The negative-classification result, which is the discriminating evidence rather than a description of the signature.

steps/4.description:
A reproducible genome-wide DNA-methylation pattern in peripheral blood, distinct from the Floating-Harbor signature and from controls.
It is included as a pathophysiology node rather than only as a laboratory test because it is the evidence that DEHMBA is a separate entity. A classifier trained on the FLHS signature calls every DEHMBA case negative, and a signature specific to the proximal-variant group emerges when the comparison is made against controls. A shared spectrum would not do that.

evidence.snippet: Through RNA sequencing, we identify dysregulation in 27 ASD-related genes in Srcap+/- mice.
evidence.explanation: Shows the dysregulated set is enriched for neurodevelopmental genes rather than being a diffuse transcriptional change.

steps/5.description: Transcriptional output at SRCAP target loci is altered. In the mouse the dysregulated set is enriched for autism-associated genes, and one target, Satb2, has been followed all the way to behaviour.

evidence.snippet: Therapeutic intervention via retro-orbital injection of adeno-associated virus (AAV)-Satb2 in neonatal Srcap+/- mice leads to amelioration of the neurodevelopmental and ASD-like abnormalities.
evidence.explanation: Rescue by restoring the depleted factor, which is what makes this node load-bearing in the model rather than merely correlated.

steps/6.description:
Satb2 - itself the gene of a distinct neurodevelopmental disorder - is expressed at reduced levels because H2A.Z occupancy at its promoter falls.
This node is mouse-only, and the entry is explicit about that. It is retained rather than dropped because it is the one branch of the mechanism with interventional support: restoring Satb2 rescues the model phenotype, which is a stronger form of evidence than correlation, and it is simultaneously the branch whose translation to human DEHMBA is unproven.

evidence.snippet: Notably, a reduction in parvalbumin-positive neurons is observed in the retrosplenial cortex (RSC) and dentate gyrus (DG) of these mice.
evidence.explanation: The cellular finding and the two regions it was made in.

evidence.snippet: In the late developmental brain, EP400 is predominantly expressed in excitatory neurons, in contrast to the higher proportion of SRCAP expression in inhibitory neurons, explaining the association of SRCAP variants with DEE and refractory FE.
evidence.explanation: Human expression data placing SRCAP preferentially in inhibitory neurons, which makes an interneuron-weighted lesion plausible in people. Indirect: an expression pattern is not a demonstration that interneurons are lost in patients.

steps/7.description: Fewer parvalbumin-positive interneurons in the retrosplenial cortex and dentate gyrus of Srcap heterozygous mice. Inhibitory interneuron loss is a recurrent cellular substrate for autism-like and social-behaviour phenotypes, and it is consistent with the independent human observation that SRCAP is expressed preferentially in inhibitory neurons of the late developmental brain.

evidence.snippet: Detailed clinical characterization of the proximal SRCAP individuals identified shared characteristics: developmental delay with or without intellectual disability, behavioral and psychiatric problems, non-specific facial features, musculoskeletal issues, and hypotonia.
evidence.explanation: The phenotype this node represents, as characterized in the founding cohort.

steps/8.description: The clinical convergence point: global developmental delay with or without intellectual disability, disproportionate speech and language delay, hypotonia, and behavioural and psychiatric problems. The course is static rather than degenerative, which is what a developmental chromatinopathy predicts and what distinguishes it from a neurometabolic differential.

evidence.snippet: Detailed clinical characterization of the proximal SRCAP individuals identified shared characteristics: developmental delay with or without intellectual disability, behavioral and psychiatric problems, non-specific facial features, musculoskeletal issues, and hypotonia.

open_questions/0.rationale:
Everything in this entry above the H2A.Z step is human: the variants, the episignature, the phenotype. Everything below it is mouse.
That is not a complaint about the mouse work, which is unusually strong - it identifies a specific target, shows the chromatin mechanism at that target's promoter, and then rescues the phenotype by restoring it. The problem is that the rescue is exactly what makes the axis tempting to state as the disease mechanism, and no part of it has been observed in a person with DEHMBA. There is no human DEHMBA brain transcriptomic or single-cell data, no measurement of SATB2 in patient tissue, and no count of parvalbumin interneurons in a human case.
The mismatch is sharper than a generic species caveat for two reasons. First, the mouse is a whole-gene heterozygous knockout, so it models haploinsufficiency in general and is blind to the exon 33-34 position rule that defines DEHMBA against Floating-Harbor syndrome - a Srcap+/- mouse is arguably a model of both diseases or of neither. Second, SATB2 haploinsufficiency causes its own well-characterized human syndrome, and DEHMBA does not resemble it, which is at least a prima facie argument that reduced SATB2 is not doing the same work in people that it does in the model.
Resolving it does not need new technology. The human iPSC lines carrying distal-locus frameshifts already exist; differentiating them and asking whether H2A.Z occupancy and SATB2 expression fall at the human promoter would settle the first half.

open_questions/1.rationale:
The disorder's name puts musculoskeletal defects on equal footing with developmental delay, and the mechanism in this entry accounts for none of them. Every mechanistic step curated here is neural: H2A.Z deposition measured in neuroblastoma cells, interneurons counted in mouse brain, behaviour assayed in mice.
The founding cohort reports musculoskeletal issues without resolving them into specific findings with frequencies, and no study has examined mesenchymal, chondrocyte or osteoblast lineages in this disease. So the gap is double: the phenotype is described too coarsely to model, and the model systems that exist are neural.
It is worth stating rather than leaving implicit, because a mechanism that explains two of the four name-bearing features and is silent on a third is an incomplete account being presented as a complete one. Note the contrast with Floating-Harbor syndrome, where the skeletal phenotype is precise - delayed bone age, brachydactyly - and the difference in skeletal involvement between the two allele classes is itself unexplained.

steps/1.description: Biallelic inactivation of SMARCB1 (INI1/BAF47/SNF5) disables a core subunit of the SWI/SNF (BAF) chromatin-remodeling complex. evidence.snippet: Over 90% of tumours have lost INI1 expression, leading to oncogenic dependence on the transcriptional repressor EZH2.

steps/2.description: SWI/SNF normally opposes Polycomb repressive complex 2 (PRC2). When SMARCB1 is lost, PRC2/EZH2 activity is unopposed, increasing trimethylation of histone H3 at lysine 27 (H3K27me3) and epigenetically repressing differentiation and tumor-suppressor genes. SMARCB1-deficient tumors become dependent on EZH2 activity, the rationale for therapeutic EZH2 inhibition.

steps/3.description: The combined loss of SWI/SNF tumor-suppressor function and the resulting epigenetic repression drive a proliferative, poorly differentiated phenotype with retained epithelial-mesenchymal hybrid marker expression, manifesting as progressive locally infiltrative tumor growth.
