evidence.snippet: Regression of achieved milestones is seen in addition to delayed milestones in most individuals with this condition.
evidence.explanation: Direct statement that regression occurs in most affected individuals.

evidence.snippet: profound psychomotor delay, developmental regression, early-onset epilepsy, microcephaly and progressive spastic tetraplegia
evidence.explanation: Regression listed as a core cohort feature.

steps/14.description: Loss of previously acquired milestones is superimposed on the delay in most individuals, and is the feature that identifies the disorder as neurodegenerative rather than purely developmental. Regression is usually early; in the mildest reported family it began only after school age.

evidence.snippet: Cognitive delay too has been consistently noted in all the reported individuals, including the individuals in our study, except for two individuals of a family reported by Saad et al.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that cognitive impairment is a consistent feature across every reported individual, with the mildest (stop-loss) family as the only exception.

evidence.snippet: Variants in these genes typically result in overlapping clinical features, including microcephaly, early-onset epilepsy, intellectual disability, neurodevelopmental regression, spasticity and abnormal brain MRI findings.
evidence.explanation: Intellectual disability listed among the core overlapping features.

steps/15.description: Cognitive impairment is severe to profound and has been noted consistently in all reported individuals other than the two siblings of the mildest reported family. The founding report characterised the phenotype as severe syndromic intellectual disability. The ungraded parent term is bound because the quotable cohort literature reports the cognitive impairment without a formal severity grade; the severity range is kept in the display name.

evidence.snippet: Early-onset seizures (two months to six months) were noted in 23 out of 31 individuals with recurrent splicing variant along with P1 (one year).
evidence.explanation: Provides both the age of onset and the quantitative denominator used for the frequency band.

evidence.snippet: profound psychomotor delay, developmental regression, early-onset epilepsy, microcephaly and progressive spastic tetraplegia
evidence.explanation: Early-onset epilepsy as a core cohort feature.

steps/16.description: Seizures are a defining feature and begin early, usually between two and six months of age and within the first year in nearly all patients. Seizure onset at seven years in the mildest reported family is the exception. Semiology includes epileptic spasms, focal, tonic, atonic and generalized tonic-clonic seizures, and control is often only partial.

evidence.snippet: A variety of seizures, including spasms, occur early in NEDESBA.
evidence.explanation: Documents spasms among the early seizure types.

evidence.snippet: Here, we report a 13-month-old affected male born to consanguineous parents, presenting with epileptic spasms and progressive neurodevelopmental delay.
evidence.explanation: Epileptic spasms as the presenting seizure type in a reported infant.

steps/17.description: Epileptic (infantile) spasms are one of the reported early seizure types and may be the presenting event, accompanied by a very low voltage EEG background.

evidence.snippet: They presented with generalized tonic-clonic seizures at seven years of age.
evidence.explanation: Documents generalized tonic-clonic seizures in reported patients.

evidence.snippet: Seizure semiology include generalized tonic-clonic seizures, staring episodes, febrile seizures and complex partial motor seizures.
evidence.explanation: Cohort-level review statement placing generalized tonic-clonic seizures in the semiology of the disorder beyond the missense families.

steps/18.description: Generalized tonic-clonic seizures are among the reported semiologies and were the presenting seizure type in the individuals with novel missense TRAPPC4 variants.

evidence.snippet: Epileptiform abnormalities, generalized disorganization and very low voltage background activity are reported.
evidence.explanation: Describes the reported EEG abnormalities.

steps/19.description: The EEG is abnormal but not specific: epileptiform discharges, generalized disorganization, and progressive background voltage suppression that parallels the developing cortical atrophy.

evidence.snippet: TRAPPC4-related neurodevelopmental disorder with epilepsy, spasticity, and brain atrophy (MIM# 618741) is a recently described TRAPPopathy with clinical findings of developmental delay, seizures, postnatal microcephaly, spasticity, facial dysmorphism, and cerebral and cerebellar atrophy.
evidence.explanation: Explicitly identifies the microcephaly as postnatal (i.e. acquired/progressive).

evidence.snippet: Patients all had progressive microcephaly due to severe brain atrophy, spastic quadriparesis, early-onset seizures, profound developmental delay
evidence.explanation: States that the microcephaly is progressive and attributes it to the underlying brain atrophy.

steps/20.description: Head circumference is usually normal or near-normal at birth and falls steeply postnatally as brain volume is lost, reaching extreme values in older children. Microcephaly is one of the most consistent features of the disorder.

evidence.snippet: profound psychomotor delay, developmental regression, early-onset epilepsy, microcephaly and progressive spastic tetraplegia
evidence.explanation: Progressive spastic tetraplegia as a core cohort feature.

evidence.snippet: microcephaly, sensorineural deafness, spastic quadriparesis and progressive cortical and cerebellar atrophy
evidence.explanation: Spastic quadriparesis in the founding cohort.

steps/21.description: Spasticity involves all four limbs, is progressive, and is accompanied by brisk deep tendon reflexes. It is a cardinal feature and contributes directly to the inability to sit or walk; it is frequently refractory to baclofen.

evidence.snippet: On re-evaluation at one year-two months, he had failure to thrive, dystonia, spasticity and brisk deep tendon reflexes.
evidence.explanation: Documents brisk deep tendon reflexes in a reported patient.

steps/22.description: Brisk deep tendon reflexes accompany the spasticity and confirm the upper-motor-neuron localization.

evidence.snippet: Involuntary movements in the form of ataxia, tremors and dystonia which were previously reported in 12 out of 33 individuals, were also noted in P1 and P2.
evidence.explanation: Documents ataxia, tremor and dystonia as the movement-disorder phenotypes of this condition. The aggregate 12-of-33 count covers all three together, so it is retained in notes rather than asserted as a frequency band on any single bound term.

steps/23.description: Dystonia is part of a mixed involuntary-movement disorder (with ataxia and tremor, each recorded separately) present in a substantial minority, reported in 12 of 33 individuals in the literature review and confirmed in subsequently reported patients.

evidence.snippet: Involuntary movements in the form of ataxia, tremors and dystonia which were previously reported in 12 out of 33 individuals
evidence.explanation: Ataxia reported among the involuntary movements in this disorder.

steps/24.description: Gait and limb ataxia occurs in the subset of patients with enough motor ability to demonstrate it, and is part of the same involuntary-movement spectrum as tremor and dystonia.

evidence.snippet: Involuntary movements in the form of ataxia, tremors and dystonia which were previously reported in 12 out of 33 individuals, were also noted in P1 and P2.
evidence.explanation: Tremor reported among the involuntary movements in this disorder.

steps/25.description: Tremor is the third element of the mixed involuntary-movement spectrum reported alongside dystonia and ataxia in a substantial minority of patients.

evidence.snippet: All individuals with NEDESBA, except for P2 and P3, either showed complete absence of motor development or had significant motor delay.
evidence.explanation: Documents the near-universal absence of motor development that precludes walking, with the mild family as the stated exception.

steps/26.description: Almost all affected individuals show complete absence of motor development or such significant motor delay that independent ambulation is never achieved.

evidence.snippet: Affected siblings attained age-appropriate motor milestones, however speech delay was noted in early childhood (three years). They could speak only small sentences at the age of five years.
evidence.explanation: Documents the language impairment, and in the mildest family shows the residual-speech end of the spectrum.

steps/27.description: Expressive language does not develop in the classic severe presentation. In the mildest reported family speech was delayed and limited to short sentences by age five, before regression.

evidence.snippet: Marked cerebral atrophy is seen in those with recurrent splicing variant and was observed in P1 in the current study.
evidence.explanation: Cerebral atrophy in patients with the recurrent variant.

evidence.snippet: Brain MRI findings show a variable degree of progressive cerebral atrophy with an increased severity in older age.
evidence.explanation: Establishes progression of the cortical atrophy with age.

steps/28.description: Progressive cerebral cortical atrophy, most marked in frontotemporal regions, is the imaging hallmark. It is present in essentially all imaged patients with the recurrent splice variant and worsens with age, with enlarged subarachnoid spaces and secondary ventricular enlargement.

evidence.snippet: Cerebellar atrophy, another significant finding reported in 21 out of 27 individuals with TRAPPC4 variant, was not observed in individuals from our study.
evidence.explanation: Supplies the numerator/denominator for the frequency band and documents that the finding is not universal.

evidence.snippet: progressive cortical and cerebellar atrophy
evidence.explanation: Cerebellar atrophy in the founding cohort.

steps/29.description: Cerebellar atrophy accompanies the cerebral atrophy in most, but not all, imaged patients; it was reported in 21 of 27 individuals in a literature review and was absent in the two Indian families with novel missense variants.

evidence.snippet: Non-specific white matter abnormalities (delayed myelination, white matter volume loss, hyperintensities in periventricular region), thin corpus callosum and ventriculomegaly are also frequent imaging findings.
evidence.explanation: Describes the white-matter findings and their frequency.

steps/30.description: White-matter involvement is non-specific but frequent: delayed myelination, white-matter volume loss, and periventricular T2/FLAIR hyperintensities.

evidence.snippet: thin corpus callosum and ventriculomegaly are also frequent imaging findings
evidence.explanation: Thin corpus callosum listed among frequent imaging findings.

steps/31.description: A thin corpus callosum is a frequent, though non-specific, accompanying imaging finding.

evidence.snippet: thin corpus callosum and ventriculomegaly are also frequent imaging findings
evidence.explanation: Ventriculomegaly listed among frequent imaging findings.

evidence.snippet: Enlarged subarachnoid spaces, loss of white matter, enlarged ventricles and cerebellar atrophy have also been reported frequently.
evidence.explanation: Independent confirmation of enlarged ventricles as a frequent finding.

steps/32.description: Ventricular enlargement is common and is largely secondary (ex vacuo) to the progressive loss of brain parenchyma.

evidence.snippet: Eye problems occur in most of the TRAPPC4 patients with absence of pursuit and optic atrophy.
evidence.explanation: Establishes visual involvement in most patients.

evidence.snippet: Hearing and ophthalmological abnormalities (cortical visual defects, no tracking, roving eye movements, nystagmus and optic atrophy) as seen in P1 are also reported in 30 out of 31 previously affected individuals
evidence.explanation: Enumerates the specific ophthalmological abnormalities reported.

steps/33.description: Visual dysfunction is near-universal and largely cortical: absent visual pursuit and tracking, roving eye movements, and cortical visual defects. Bilateral cataracts have been reported in a small number of patients.

evidence.snippet: Our patient also developed optic atrophy, which was not present at the first ophthalmological examination.
evidence.explanation: Documents the acquired, progressive nature of the optic atrophy.

steps/34.description: Optic atrophy develops during the course of the illness rather than being present at first assessment, mirroring the progressive nature of the disorder.

evidence.snippet: P1 presented in the early infantile period with developmental delay, feeding difficulties and seizures as observed in most of the individuals with recurrent splicing TRAPPC4 variant
evidence.explanation: Documents feeding difficulties as an early presenting feature seen in most individuals with the recurrent variant.

steps/35.description: Feeding difficulties, including regurgitation of feeds from the newborn period, are an early consequence of the profound neurological impairment and are a common reason for enteral feeding support.

evidence.snippet: On re-evaluation at one year-two months, he had failure to thrive, dystonia, spasticity and brisk deep tendon reflexes.
evidence.explanation: Failure to thrive documented in a reported patient.

steps/36.description: Poor weight gain and failure to thrive follow from the feeding difficulties and the overall severity of the encephalopathy.

evidence.snippet: Elevated CPK were also observed in P1 and P3, thus reiterating the significance of assessing CPK levels for this condition.
evidence.explanation: Documents elevated creatine kinase in reported patients.

evidence.snippet: However, our patient had normal serum CK and lactate levels without any muscle involvement.
evidence.explanation: Counter-example establishing that CK elevation and muscle involvement are not universal features.

steps/37.description: A subset of patients has laboratory evidence of muscle involvement, with persistently or episodically elevated serum creatine kinase, in one instance amounting to probable episodic rhabdomyolysis. Muscle involvement is a recurring theme across the TRAPPopathies and its presence should prompt CK measurement, but it is not universal: CK was normal in other reported patients.

edges/1.description: The recurrent c.454+3A>G allele acts at the RNA level, disrupting the splice donor of exon 3.

edges/2.description: Muscle involvement recurs across the TRAPPopathies and is documented in TRAPPC4 patients with more than one allele class, but the intermediate steps from reduced TRAPPC4 to muscle-fibre damage have not been studied.

edges/3.description: Less full-length TRAPPC4 protein is available to incorporate into the TRAPP complex.

edges/4.description: The GEF active site is formed across several core subunits, so a destabilized complex has reduced exchange activity.

edges/5.description: RAB1-GTP is required to tether COPII vesicles at the cis-Golgi.

edges/6.description: RAB1 is required for the first step of macroautophagy.

edges/7.description: Chronic secretory-pathway impairment is presumed to be poorly tolerated by long-lived, highly polarized neurons.

edges/8.description: Post-mitotic neurons depend on autophagy for proteostasis and cannot dilute undegraded cargo by division.

edges/9.description: The intermediate steps linking trafficking failure to seizure generation in this disorder are not established.

edges/10.description: Cumulative neuronal proteostatic failure is the presumed but untested driver of the atrophy.

edges/11.description: Upper-motor-neuron involvement follows cortical and white-matter loss.

edges/12.description: Early-onset, poorly controlled epileptic activity contributes to the developmental arrest characteristic of an epileptic encephalopathy.

edges/13.description: Recurrent early-onset seizures are the direct clinical expression of the cortical hyperexcitability.

edges/14.description: Epileptic spasms are among the early seizure types produced by the hyperexcitable cortex and may be the presenting event.

edges/15.description: Generalized tonic-clonic seizures are part of the varied semiology arising from the hyperexcitable cortical network.

edges/16.description: Epileptiform discharges and generalized background disorganization are the electrographic signature of the hyperexcitable cortex.

edges/17.description: Spastic tetraplegia is a direct barrier to the acquisition of motor milestones such as sitting and walking.

edges/18.description: Progressive four-limb spasticity is the direct clinical expression of the upper-motor-neuron dysfunction.

edges/19.description: Brisk deep tendon reflexes are the accompanying upper-motor-neuron sign of the same corticospinal dysfunction.

edges/20.description: Ongoing loss of brain volume underlies the loss of previously acquired milestones.

edges/21.description: Cortical volume loss on serial MRI is the direct imaging readout of the degenerative process.

edges/22.description: Cerebellar volume loss accompanies the cerebral atrophy in most imaged patients as part of the same degenerative process.

evidence.snippet: Patients all had progressive microcephaly due to severe brain atrophy
evidence.explanation: Explicit causal attribution of the progressive microcephaly to the brain atrophy.

edges/23.description: Progressive postnatal head-growth failure is the skull-circumference correlate of the underlying brain volume loss.

edges/24.description: White-matter volume loss with periventricular signal change is the white-matter arm of the progressive parenchymal loss.

edges/25.description: Callosal thinning accompanies the diffuse white-matter volume loss.

evidence.snippet: lateral ventricles and subarachnoid spaces are enlarged, secondary to atrophy at the age of 5.5 months
evidence.explanation: Imaging report attributing the ventricular and subarachnoid-space enlargement to the atrophy.

edges/26.description: Ventricular enlargement is largely ex vacuo, secondary to the progressive loss of brain parenchyma.

edges/27.description: Optic atrophy appears during follow-up having been absent at first examination, but its route — primary optic nerve degeneration versus retrograde/trans-synaptic loss from the degenerating visual cortex — has not been established in any reported patient.

edges/28.description: The visual dysfunction is largely cortical, reflecting degeneration of the visual cortex, with optic atrophy contributing in a subset.

edges/29.description: The progressive background voltage suppression on EEG tracks the advancing cortical atrophy.

edges/30.description: Cerebellar degeneration is the presumed substrate of the ataxia seen in patients with sufficient residual motor function.

edges/31.description: The anatomical substrate of the mixed movement disorder has not been localized; it is presumed to reflect the diffuse degenerative process.

edges/32.description: The anatomical substrate of the mixed movement disorder has not been localized; it is presumed to reflect the diffuse degenerative process.

edges/33.description: Profound global developmental delay is the clinical expression of the near-complete arrest of psychomotor development.

edges/34.description: Loss of the few milestones that were attained is the regressive component of the arrested trajectory.

edges/35.description: Absent psychomotor progress translates into severe cognitive impairment in all but the mildest reported family.

edges/36.description: Expressive language fails to develop as part of the global developmental arrest.

edges/37.description: Complete absence of motor development, compounded by the spastic tetraplegia, precludes independent ambulation.

edges/38.description: Feeding difficulties, present from the newborn period in some patients, are an early consequence of the profound neurological impairment.

edges/39.description: Poor weight gain follows from the feeding difficulties and the overall severity of the encephalopathy.

edges/40.description: Creatine kinase released from damaged muscle fibres is the laboratory readout of the muscle involvement.

evidence.snippet: This is the first report of a TRAPPC4 variant, and our findings add to the growing number of TRAPP-associated neurological disorders.
evidence.explanation: The founding gene-disease association.

evidence.snippet: These data confirm the pathogenicity of the TRAPPC4 c.454+3A>G variant, and refine the clinical presentation of TRAPPC4-related encephalopathy.
evidence.explanation: Independent multicentre confirmation of the gene-disease relationship.

evidence.snippet: of the 33 individuals from 22 families reported to date, 31 individuals from 21 families have been reported with a recurrent homozygous pathogenic variant
evidence.explanation: Quantifies how strongly the allelic spectrum is dominated by one variant.

evidence.snippet: Further, I-Mutant also predicts the decreased stability of the mutant protein
evidence.explanation: In silico stability prediction supporting the destabilizing effect of the p.(Leu64Pro) missense allele; classified COMPUTATIONAL because it is a prediction, not a measurement.

genes/0.notes: TRAPPC4 (aliases SBDN, synbindin, TRS23) lies at 11q23.3 and encodes one of the small core subunits shared by the TRAPPII and TRAPPIII complexes. The allelic spectrum is unusually narrow. The recurrent non-canonical splice variant NM_016146.5:c.454+3A>G (hg19:chr11:g.118890966A>G; hg38:11:119020256 A>G; ClinVar VCV000812649.1) accounts for 31 of 33 reported individuals from 21 of 22 families, almost always homozygous and usually in a consanguineous setting; a screen of over 10,000 patients with neurodevelopmental conditions found no other clinically relevant TRAPPC4 variant. The remaining reported alleles are two novel homozygous missense variants in Indian families, c.191T>C p.(Leu64Pro) and c.278C>T p.(Pro93Leu) (both predicted to destabilize the protein), and a biallelic in-frame deletion causing stop-loss in one family with a milder, later-onset phenotype and normal head circumference. All are hypomorphic: complete loss of this essential core subunit is thought to be incompatible with survival. Penetrance: every reported homozygote for c.454+3A>G has been clinically affected, so penetrance appears complete for that genotype; heterozygous carriers are unaffected. Penetrance across the wider (very small) allelic spectrum is not established, and no unaffected homozygote has been described. The residual level of correctly spliced transcript is the presumed determinant of both viability and severity, but this has not been measured against clinical severity in a patient series.

evidence.snippet: She was put on levetiracetam (LEV) treatment, although infrequent clonic seizures occurred despite LEV therapy of 40 mg/kg/day.
evidence.explanation: Documents levetiracetam use and the incomplete response that motivated a drug change.

evidence.snippet: She had had no obvious seizure on topiramate treatment of 5 mg/kg/day.
evidence.explanation: Documents seizure control achieved after switching to topiramate.

treatments/0.description: Symptomatic treatment of the epilepsy. Levetiracetam, topiramate, clobazam and valproate have all been used; responses are frequently partial and seizures may persist or recur despite escalation, so drug substitution is common. No disease-modifying therapy exists.

evidence.snippet: persistent spasticity in spite of baclofen treatment and a physical rehabilitation program were noted
evidence.explanation: Documents baclofen plus rehabilitation as the treatment used, and its limited effect.

treatments/1.description: Antispasticity pharmacotherapy, in reported practice baclofen, combined with a physical rehabilitation programme. Reported responses are poor: spasticity persisted despite baclofen and rehabilitation in a documented patient, so expectations should be set accordingly.

evidence.snippet: persistent spasticity in spite of baclofen treatment and a physical rehabilitation program were noted
evidence.explanation: Documents that a physical rehabilitation programme forms part of management.

treatments/2.description: Multidisciplinary physical, occupational and communication therapy for the profound motor and developmental impairment. Rehabilitation is supportive and does not alter the progressive course.

evidence.snippet: P1 presented in the early infantile period with developmental delay, feeding difficulties and seizures
evidence.explanation: Establishes the feeding difficulty that this supportive measure addresses.

treatments/3.description: Management of feeding difficulties, regurgitation and failure to thrive, with enteral or tube feeding when oral intake becomes unsafe or insufficient.

evidence.snippet: Carrier frequency of this neurodevelopmental and neurodegenerative disorder, NEDESBA, has been reported to be relatively high, varying from 2.4-5.4 per 10 000 individuals worldwide
evidence.explanation: The carrier frequency that makes cascade testing and carrier screening a meaningful part of counseling.

evidence.snippet: Given a relatively high carrier frequency, it is crucial to recognize and consider this diagnosis.
evidence.explanation: Independent statement of the counseling/recognition imperative.

treatments/4.description: Autosomal recessive inheritance carries a 25% recurrence risk for each subsequent pregnancy. Because the recurrent c.454+3A>G allele has a measurable carrier frequency in the general population, on the order of a few per 10,000 and highest in Mediterranean and European ancestries, cascade carrier testing of relatives and, once the familial allele is known, prenatal or preimplantation testing are the practical preventive options.

open_questions/0.rationale: These four phenotypes are well documented in the cohorts but none has an established mechanistic route from the trafficking/autophagy defect, so no causal edge is asserted for them. Delayed myelination is a failure of a developmental process rather than degeneration, and oligodendrocyte biology has not been examined in this disorder. The sensorineural deafness has no published localization (cochlear hair cell versus auditory nerve versus central). Nystagmus with roving eye movements in a blind infant is commonly sensory, but no source makes that attribution here, and cerebellar or brainstem origins are equally unexcluded. Elevated lactate prompted mitochondrial workups that were negative, and it is unclear whether it is muscle-derived (it co-occurred with elevated creatine kinase in one patient) or reflects another metabolic derangement. All cellular studies to date used dermal fibroblasts, so none of these lineage-specific questions has been addressed in a relevant cell type.

open_questions/1.rationale: The subtle facial gestalt (bitemporal narrowing, thick eyebrows, full cheeks, long philtrum, pointed chin) is recurrently described in patients with the recurrent splice variant, but no craniofacial developmental mechanism has been proposed or studied, and bitemporal narrowing in particular may simply track the severe progressive microcephaly. No causal edge is asserted for these phenotypes; connecting them would require developmental data that do not exist for this gene.

open_questions/2.rationale: Frequent infections are the stated usual cause of death, yet no immune phenotyping has been reported beyond a single patient with low IgA and atopic dermatitis, whose reporting authors themselves suggested that searching for immunodeficiency in these patients might expand the phenotype. Membrane trafficking is integral to immune-cell secretion and antigen handling, so a primary component is biologically plausible, but on current evidence no causal edge can be asserted and the phenotype is left unconnected.

evidence.snippet: Exome sequencing led us to identify bi-allelic loss of function variants in VWA1 as the molecular cause underlying a so far genetically undefined neuromuscular disorder.
evidence.explanation: Establishes biallelic VWA1 loss of function as the molecular cause of the condition.

evidence.snippet: A single disease-associated allele p.(G25Rfs*74), a 10-bp repeat expansion, was observed in 14/15 families and was homozygous in 10/15.
evidence.explanation: Identifies the recurrent founder allele and its frequency within the first reported cohort.

steps/1.description: Two loss-of-function alleles of VWA1, the gene encoding the extracellular matrix protein WARP. Reported alleles are predominantly frameshifts and stop-gains, with a small number of missense changes affecting proline residues; the disease-defining allele is the 10 bp exon 1 duplication NM_022834.5:c.62_71dup p.(Gly25ArgfsTer74), which was present in 14 of 15 families in the first reported cohort and in 12 of 15 families in the 2024 cohort. Both homozygosity for that allele and compound heterozygosity for it in trans with a second truncating variant are common.

evidence.snippet: However, there was no detectable VWA1 in either the conditioned medium or cell layer of the patient’s fibroblast
evidence.explanation: Direct demonstration that the patient cell makes no detectable WARP protein to secrete or deposit.

evidence.snippet: A high level of VWA1 was detected in mouse sciatic nerve extraction. In the primary culture of mouse sciatic nerve, VWA1 was detectable in its cell layer (cytoplasm and ECM) but not in the conditioned medium, indicating the secreted VWA1 was able to deposit as ECM efficiently.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that the protein lost in patients is normally abundant in peripheral nerve and is deposited into the matrix there.

steps/2.description: Transcripts carrying the premature termination codon are partially degraded by nonsense-mediated decay, and no WARP protein is detectable in patient dermal fibroblasts in either the cell layer or the conditioned medium, whereas control fibroblasts secrete detectable protein. In the mouse the protein is abundant in sciatic nerve and is efficiently deposited into the matrix, so the human null state removes a protein that is normally present at the site of disease.

evidence.snippet: WARP is expressed in the vasculature of neural tissues and in basement membrane structures of the peripheral nervous system. Furthermore, WARP is also expressed in the apical ectodermal ridge of developing limb buds, and in skeletal and cardiac muscle.
evidence.explanation: The reporter-gene study that established where WARP sits — peripheral nerve basement membrane and skeletal muscle — which is what this node claims is depleted.

evidence.snippet: Further ultrastructural analysis revealed reduced fibrillar collagen deposition within the peripheral nerve extracellular matrix and abnormal partial fusing of adjacent Schwann cell basement membranes, suggesting an important function for WARP in stabilizing the association of the collagenous interstitial matrix with the Schwann cell basement membrane.
evidence.explanation: The primary ultrastructural result defining the lesion at this node, and the authors' own statement of what WARP does there.

evidence.snippet: Immunostaining of WARP-interacting ligands demonstrated that the collagen VI microfibrillar matrix was severely reduced and mislocalized in peripheral nerves of WARP-null mice.
evidence.explanation: Shows that WARP loss disorganises the collagen VI matrix specifically in nerve, which is the mechanistic content of this node's nerve arm.

evidence.snippet: The von Willebrand factor A-domain-related protein (WARP) encoded by the VWA1 gene, is an orphan extracellular matrix protein that is expressed in a subset of ECM structures but whose function is poorly understood.
evidence.explanation: A review of the protein confirms its restricted matrix distribution and records that its normal function is not well understood, which bounds how strongly any mechanism below this node can be stated.

steps/3.description: WARP is expressed in the basement membrane structures of the peripheral nervous system and is most abundant, among human tissues surveyed, in tibial nerve. Its loss leaves the nerve basement membrane structurally abnormal: electron microscopy of WARP-deficient mouse sciatic nerve shows partial fusion of the basement membranes of neighbouring axons, and collagen VI is reduced in regions of the peripheral nerve matrix. WARP is co-expressed with collagen VI in the endomysium of muscle, so the same deficit exists on the muscle side, but the mouse showed no histological or behavioural muscle pathology and collagen VI labelling is normal in patient muscle — which is why the muscle arm of this node is curated as contested rather than established.

evidence.snippet: CRISPR and morpholino vwa1 modelling in zebrafish demonstrated reductions in motor neuron axonal growth, synaptic formation in the skeletal muscles and locomotive behaviour.
evidence.explanation: Summarises the three model readouts that define this node — axon growth, synapse formation, and locomotion.

evidence.snippet: Phenotypic assessment of the vwa1 crispants/morphants demonstrated a prominent effect on motor neurons including shorter axons and abnormal growth.
evidence.explanation: The primary axon-growth observation behind this node.

steps/4.description: In the zebrafish model, loss of the vwa1 orthologue significantly reduces spinal motor neuron growth measured across days 2 to 4 of development, with aberrant axon structures from day 3, sparser and disorganised myofibres, and significantly reduced synapse formation in skeletal muscle measured by acetylcholine receptor staining, followed by reduced locomotive behaviour. This places the defect early — at the point where motor axons grow out and form endplates — rather than at a later dying-back stage, which fits the human observation that foot deformity and tendon contracture are present from the first years of life and were congenital in two cases.

evidence.snippet: Motor nerve action potentials from the lower limb nerves were reduced or undetectable with uniformly preserved conduction velocities. Sensory studies were overall normal.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the lesion as motor axon loss rather than demyelination or a sensorimotor process.

evidence.snippet: In almost half of those cases, weakness was more pronounced proximally, and one-quarter had equally weak proximal and distal muscle groups, raising the clinical suspicion of non-length dependent motor axonal neuropathy.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the non-length-dependent distribution that separates this disease from the rest of the dHMN family.

evidence.snippet: Distal hereditary motor neuropathies (dHMN) are a clinically and genetically diverse group of disorders that are characterized by length-dependent axonal degeneration of lower motor neurons.
evidence.explanation: Gives the family definition this disease departs from: length-dependence is the defining feature of the dHMNs in general, and is absent here.

steps/5.description: Loss of motor axons producing reduced or absent compound motor action potentials with preserved conduction velocities — an axonal, not demyelinating, motor neuropathy — and normal sensory studies in most patients. The distinguishing feature of this disease is that the loss is not graded by axon length: three-quarters of the first cohort had simultaneous proximal and distal lower limb weakness, and in almost half of those the proximal weakness was the more severe. That is the opposite of the distal-first gradient that defines most of the distal hereditary motor neuropathies, and it is why this entry does not conform to the length-dependent peripheral axonal degeneration module.

evidence.snippet: Muscle ultrasound of the left tibialis anterior from the same patient shows a moth-eaten pattern consisting of round, dark areas with remaining viable motor units, surrounded by tissue with increased greyscale level reflecting permanently denervated and fibrosed muscle tissue.
evidence.explanation: Describes denervated muscle tissue directly, with the imaging correlate of surviving versus lost motor units.

evidence.snippet: Muscle biopsies were performed in seven cases, of which four were available for review (Fig. 3). In 4/7 of these, clear neurogenic changes were reported.
evidence.explanation: Gives the proportion of biopsies showing neurogenic change in the first cohort.

steps/6.description: Muscle downstream of the lost motor axons undergoes denervation with partial reinnervation, producing the classical morphological signature: fibre type grouping, fascicular grouping of type 1 fibres, and neurogenic atrophy, with a moth-eaten pattern on muscle ultrasound in long-standing denervation without reinnervation. Four of seven biopsies in the first cohort showed clear neurogenic changes.

evidence.snippet: Plasma proteomics unravelled dysregulation of 15 proteins serving as biomarker candidates among which a profound proportion of increased ones (6/11) are mostly related to antioxidative processes and have even partially been described as blood biomarkers for other entities of neuromuscular disorders before.
evidence.explanation: Reports the plasma protein signature attributed to the disease, weighted toward antioxidative processes.

steps/7.description: An abnormality of the muscle extracellular space itself in patients lacking WARP, independent of any denervation. Proteomic profiling of patient white blood cells, plasma and muscle reported increased C-reactive protein in the extracellular space of VWA1-mutant muscle and increased NEFM in cells within the muscle matrix of every patient biopsy examined, and the plasma signature was dominated by proteins related to antioxidative processes. This node exists only under the alternative hypothesis that the muscle is a primary target; it is not asserted under the canonical model.

evidence.snippet: In the other three biopsies there was evidence for myopathic features in addition to findings suggestive of an underlying neurogenic process.
evidence.explanation: Records the coexistence of myopathic and neurogenic features in the same biopsies.

evidence.snippet: Histological data were available for three cases, revealing a dystrophic pattern in one with multiple ring fibres, while the other two exhibited extensive fibre grouping indicative of neurogenic changes.
evidence.explanation: Gives the proportion of biopsies that were dystrophic rather than neurogenic in the second cohort.

steps/8.description: Myopathic features in patient muscle: a dystrophic pattern with ring fibres in one biopsy, fibre lobulation and whorling of myofibrils in another, marked variation in fibre size with increased endomysial fibrosis and perimysial fatty infiltration, rimmed vacuoles in one case, myopathic motor units on needle EMG in a minority, and raised creatine kinase in most patients. Both hypothesis groups converge on this node; they differ only in what produces it.

evidence.snippet: Available nerve conduction studies typically revealed findings consistent with a motor axonal neuropathy which was often interpreted as suggestive of a distal spinal muscular atrophy/hereditary motor neuropathy.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the motor axonal pattern and the diagnostic label it is usually given.

evidence.snippet: Three isolated cases had an abnormal sensory examination and this was supported by neurophysiological evidence in only one of them showing asymmetrical sural nerve involvement (Family 6).
evidence.explanation: Quantifies how uncommon sensory involvement is, which is what keeps this a motor rather than sensorimotor neuropathy.

steps/9.description: A pure or predominantly motor axonal neuropathy on nerve conduction studies: motor action potentials reduced or absent with conduction velocities preserved, and sensory studies normal in most patients. It is the finding on which the diagnosis is built. Sensory involvement is the exception rather than the rule — three of seventeen in the first cohort had an abnormal sensory examination, supported neurophysiologically in only one, and three of twenty in the second cohort had sensory involvement.

evidence.snippet: Bilateral foot drop, impaired toe walking, forward posture, and wasting in the lower limbs were frequently observed signs.
evidence.explanation: Records bilateral foot drop as a frequent sign in the first cohort.

steps/10.description: Foot drop from weakness of ankle dorsiflexion, usually bilateral and usually the presenting sign. In the second cohort all cases but two had distal lower limb weakness, mostly foot drop; one patient had one-sided foot drop with pes cavus on one foot and pes planus on the other, so asymmetry is possible.

evidence.snippet: The age of onset varied from birth to 12 years, with consistent early involvement of the distal lower limbs, presenting as various foot deformities, gait disturbances, frequent falls and ankle contractures.
evidence.explanation: Records consistent early distal lower limb involvement and the range of onset ages.

steps/11.description: Weakness of the distal leg muscles, the most severely affected group in the second cohort, with strength for toe and foot dorsiflexion or plantarflexion ranging from MRC grade 1 to 3.

evidence.snippet: While the most common features of VWA1-related disease include foot drop, foot deformities and distal lower limb weakness, about half of the so far reported individuals develop proximal leg weakness over time, and approximately one-third experience upper limb involvement
evidence.explanation: Gives the proportion developing proximal leg weakness across all reported patients.

evidence.snippet: A newly identified subtype of hereditary axonal motor neuropathy, characterized by early proximal limb involvement, has been discovered in a cohort of 34 individuals with biallelic variants in von Willebrand factor A domain-containing 1 (VWA1).
evidence.explanation: Names early proximal limb involvement as the characterising feature of the entity.

steps/12.description: Weakness of the hip and thigh muscles, present simultaneously with the distal weakness rather than following it, and in almost half of those patients more pronounced than the distal weakness. This is the feature that makes the neuropathy non-length-dependent and is the main reason the condition is mistaken for spinal muscular atrophy with lower-extremity predominance. About half of all reported individuals develop it.

evidence.snippet: ranging from pes cavus (65%, 11/17) to talipes equinovarus (35%, 6/17)
evidence.explanation: Gives the exact frequency of pes cavus in the first cohort.

steps/13.description: High-arched foot, the commoner of the two foot deformities, in 11 of 17 patients in the first cohort.

evidence.snippet: Independent walking in the cohort was achieved by the mean age of 1.6 ± 0.8 years and it was remarkably delayed in cases with foot deformities such as severe bilateral equinovarus (18%, 3/17).
evidence.explanation: Records severe bilateral equinovarus and its effect on the age of independent walking.

steps/14.description: Club foot, the more severe deformity, in 6 of 17 patients in the first cohort. Severe bilateral equinovarus was associated with markedly delayed independent walking.

evidence.snippet: Less frequent but present in more than half of the cohort were flexion tendon contractures typically involving foot plantar flexion, knee, and hip flexion but in some cases, it was also present in the major joints of the upper limbs.
evidence.explanation: Gives the frequency and distribution of the contractures.

steps/15.description: Contracture of the calcaneal tendon, among the earliest features and congenital in two reported cases. Flexion contractures were present in more than half the first cohort, typically at the ankle, knee and hip, and in some patients also in the upper limb joints.

evidence.snippet: The mean age of symptom recognition was 2.0 ± 1.4 years with tip-toe walking, foot deformities, Achilles tendon contractures, and recurrent hip and patellar dislocations.
evidence.explanation: Names tip-toe walking among the presenting features and dates it.

steps/16.description: Walking on the forefoot, recognised at a mean age of 2 years alongside the foot deformities.

evidence.snippet: Tendon reflexes were diminished in half of the cohort
evidence.explanation: Gives the frequency of diminished reflexes.

steps/17.description: Diminished tendon reflexes, in half of the first cohort.

evidence.snippet: One-third of the cases experienced frequent falls
evidence.explanation: Gives the frequency of falls in the first cohort.

steps/18.description: Frequent falls in a third of the first cohort; despite them, ambulation is usually preserved lifelong.

evidence.snippet: the condition may go unnoticed for years to decades due to its relatively benign nature, often presenting mild neurological deficits, the absence of prominent muscle atrophy and slow disease progression
evidence.explanation: States both the mildness of the atrophy and the diagnostic consequence of it.

steps/19.description: Muscle wasting, mild and predominantly in the distal legs; prominent atrophy is characteristically absent, which is part of why the condition goes unrecognised for years.

evidence.snippet: EMG typically showed chronic neurogenic changes without active denervation (10/12).
evidence.explanation: Gives the exact proportion of EMG studies showing chronic neurogenic change.

steps/20.description: Chronic neurogenic change on needle EMG without active denervation, in 10 of 12 studies in the first cohort.

evidence.snippet: Three EMG studies were reported to suggest myopathic features, albeit for two of them the formal report was unavailable.
evidence.explanation: Gives the count of myopathic EMG studies and the authors' own caveat about two of them.

steps/21.description: Myopathic motor unit potentials on needle EMG in a minority of patients — three of the first cohort's EMG studies, and one of twenty in the second. Together with the neurogenic change in the same patients this is the mixed neurogenic-and-myopathic EMG pattern that is the clinical signature of the condition, and which the differential-diagnosis literature lists VWA1 among the causes of.

evidence.snippet: In six affected individuals, creatine kinase levels were elevated (369–1628 IU/l).
evidence.explanation: Gives the count and the measured range in the first cohort.

evidence.snippet: Blood tests unveiled elevated creatine kinase (CK) levels in the majority of cases, with the highest value reaching up to 2400 U/L.
evidence.explanation: Gives the frequency and maximum value in the second cohort.

steps/22.description: Raised serum creatine kinase, in six of the first cohort at 369-1628 IU/l and in the majority of the second cohort with a maximum of 2400 U/L. It is the routine laboratory finding that most often redirects the workup toward a muscle disease.

evidence.snippet: the other two exhibited extensive fibre grouping indicative of neurogenic changes
evidence.explanation: Records fibre grouping in patient biopsies and names its neurogenic significance.

steps/23.description: Grouping of fibre types within the fascicle on muscle biopsy, the histological signature of denervation followed by reinnervation.

evidence.snippet: Unique features of VWA1 disease include scapular winging, tongue fasciculations and, recently reported,7 pyramidal signs such as upgoing plantars and/or spasticity in the lower limbs.
evidence.explanation: Names tongue fasciculation among the distinguishing features of the condition.

steps/24.description: Mild tongue fasciculation or atrophy, in two adults in the first cohort and two patients in the second. It is a feature that pushes the differential toward juvenile amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, which is one of the ways the diagnosis is missed.

evidence.snippet: Images show marked fibre hypertrophy and increased fibrosis with endo and perimysial fatty infiltration.
evidence.explanation: Describes the endomysial and perimysial change in a named patient biopsy.

steps/25.description: Increased endomysial connective tissue on muscle biopsy, with perimysial and endomysial fatty infiltration. Wired from the myopathic-change node, which is where the sources report it. It does not by itself settle which mechanism produced it: the same biopsies also show thickening of the endomysium and perimysium attributed to the chronic neurogenic process.

evidence.snippet: Duplex reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction and immunoblotting using patient fibroblasts revealed that the founder allele results in partial nonsense mediated decay and an absence of detectable protein.
evidence.explanation: Connects the founder allele directly to transcript decay and loss of the protein product.

edges/1.description: The founder duplication shifts the reading frame and introduces a premature stop 74 codons downstream, and patient fibroblasts show both reduced transcript rescued by a nonsense-mediated decay inhibitor and no detectable protein.

evidence.snippet: The von Willebrand Factor A domain containing 1 protein, encoded by VWA1, is an extracellular matrix protein expressed in muscle and peripheral nerve. It interacts with collagen VI and perlecan, two proteins that are affected in hereditary neuromuscular disorders.
evidence.explanation: States where the protein normally resides and what it binds; the citing paper is restating established protein biology rather than reporting it, hence BACKGROUND.

evidence.snippet: WARP interacts with perlecan, and we also demonstrate here that WARP binds type VI collagen, suggesting a function in bridging connective tissue structures.
evidence.explanation: The primary binding result behind the two partner proteins named throughout this entry, and the authors' proposed bridging function.

edges/2.description: WARP is an extracellular matrix protein of muscle and peripheral nerve that binds collagen VI and perlecan, so an undetectable protein is an absent matrix constituent at those sites.

evidence.snippet: These results established that vwa1 is required for the proper organization of skeletal muscles and in the formation of neuromuscular junctions.
evidence.explanation: The authors' own conclusion from the zebrafish experiments linking loss of the gene to muscle organization and endplate formation.

edges/3.description: Knockdown and knockout of the zebrafish orthologue shorten spinal motor axons and reduce acetylcholine receptor clustering in skeletal muscle, placing the matrix deficit upstream of motor axon growth and endplate formation.

evidence.snippet: Lack of VWA1 is known to compromise peripheral nerves in a Vwa1 knock-out mouse model.
evidence.explanation: States that removing the protein damages peripheral nerve in vivo; the result is the cited knockout study's, restated here as background.

edges/4.description: WARP loss compromises peripheral nerve structure and function in the knockout mouse, and the human null state produces a motor axonal neuropathy; the steps between the abnormal nerve basement membrane and axon loss are not established.

evidence.snippet: CRP elevated in plasma also showed an increase in the extracellular space of VWA1-mutant muscle.
evidence.explanation: Reports an abnormality of the muscle extracellular space itself in patients lacking WARP.

edges/5.description: Under the primary-muscle-lesion model, loss of WARP from the endomysial matrix is itself the muscle insult. This edge belongs to that hypothesis group and is not asserted under the canonical model.

evidence.snippet: Overall, the defective myofibres’ organization, neuromuscular junctions, secondary motor neuron impairment and reduced larval locomotion may reflect the early vwa1 neuropathy.
evidence.explanation: The authors' own statement that the developmental findings are what the neuropathy amounts to in this model; the hedged wording is why this edge is typed as having unknown intermediates.

edges/6.description: A developmental deficit in motor axon growth and endplate formation is offered by the authors as the origin of the human motor neuropathy, but the route from an early developmental deficit to progressive adult axon loss is not worked out.

evidence.snippet: Nerve conduction studies consistently indicated axonal motor neuropathy with sensory involvement in three cases, accompanied by chronic neuropathic changes in needle EMG.
evidence.explanation: Confirms the axonal motor pattern across the second large cohort.

edges/7.description: Axon loss with preserved conduction velocity is what the nerve conduction study records.

evidence.snippet: The most pronounced weakness was observed in the distal lower limbs, with muscle strength ranging from Grades 1 to 3 for toe and foot dorsiflexion or plantarflexion.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the distal lower limb weakness that the motor axon loss produces.

edges/8.description: Loss of the motor axons supplying the distal leg muscles.

evidence.snippet: Most of the cases (75%) were found to have simultaneous proximal and distal lower limb weakness on neurological follow-up.
evidence.explanation: Establishes proximal involvement as a majority finding rather than a late complication.

edges/9.description: The same axon loss reaches proximal motor units without an intervening distal-to-proximal progression, which is the non-length-dependent feature.

evidence.snippet: Foot drop, foot deformities and distal leg weakness followed by early proximal leg weakness are confirmed to be initial manifestations.
evidence.explanation: Names foot drop as an initial manifestation of the motor axon loss.

edges/10.description: Weakness of ankle dorsiflexion producing foot drop, the commonest presenting sign.

evidence.snippet: Tendon reflexes were diminished in half of the cohort, and muscle tone was largely reported to be normal along with uniformly negative Babinski sign.
evidence.explanation: Records the diminished reflexes, and in the same sentence the normal tone and negative plantars of the original cohort.

edges/11.description: The motor axon is the efferent limb of the tendon reflex arc, so its loss reduces the reflex; reflexes were diminished in half of the first cohort.

evidence.snippet: Two adult cases (Families 1 and 3) had shown mild tongue fasciculations or atrophy
evidence.explanation: Records the sign and its frequency in the first cohort.

edges/12.description: Reported in a minority of adults and grouped by both cohorts with the motor-neuron features of the disease; no study localises the lesion for this sign, so the edge is typed as indirect.

evidence.snippet: EMG typically showed chronic neurogenic changes without active denervation (10/12).
evidence.explanation: Gives the electrophysiological signature of chronic denervation and its frequency.

edges/13.description: Motor axon loss denervates the muscle fibres of the affected motor units; needle EMG shows chronic neurogenic change without active denervation in most patients, the picture of long-standing denervation with reinnervation.

evidence.snippet: accompanied by chronic neuropathic changes in needle EMG
evidence.explanation: Confirms chronic neurogenic needle-EMG change in the second cohort.

edges/14.description: Chronic denervation with reinnervation is what needle EMG records in most patients.

evidence.snippet: Muscle biopsy of the vastus lateralis muscle of Patient 8 shows extensive neurogenic abnormalities with many areas of fibre type grouping seen by ATPase (pH 4.6) staining.
evidence.explanation: Records fibre type grouping in patient muscle and names it a neurogenic abnormality.

edges/15.description: Reinnervation of denervated fibres by surviving motor units regroups fibre types within the fascicle.

evidence.snippet: Mild muscle atrophy, predominantly affecting the distal legs, was common.
evidence.explanation: Records the distribution and frequency of the atrophy.

edges/16.description: Denervation atrophy, predominantly of the distal leg muscles.

evidence.snippet: Hence, neurogenic muscle changes seem to be common in the VWA1 presentation, and it is likely for the observed myopathic process in a few cases to develop on the background of chronic muscle denervation.
evidence.explanation: States the causal claim this edge makes, in the authors' own words, including their hedge.

edges/17.description: Under the canonical model, the myopathic findings arise on the background of chronic denervation rather than from a second primary lesion. This edge belongs to that hypothesis group.

evidence.snippet: Our findings establish VWA1 as a new disease gene confidently implicated in this autosomal recessive neuromyopathic condition presenting with child-/adult-onset muscle weakness as a key clinical feature.
evidence.explanation: The cohort that treats the condition as a neuromyopathy, i.e. as having a muscle disease component in its own right.

edges/18.description: Under the primary-lesion model the matrix abnormality is what makes the muscle myopathic. No study has demonstrated the intervening steps.

evidence.snippet: Myopathic EMG pattern was described in only one individual.
evidence.explanation: Records how uncommon the myopathic EMG pattern was in the 20-patient cohort.

edges/19.description: Myopathic motor unit potentials on needle EMG, reported in a minority of patients in both cohorts.

evidence.snippet: Marked variation in fibres size and increased endomysial fibrosis with mostly perimysial fatty infiltration.
evidence.explanation: Reports the endomysial fibrosis alongside the fibre-size variation that defines a myopathic biopsy.

edges/20.description: Endomysial fibrosis with perimysial and endomysial fatty infiltration is one of the myopathic biopsy features listed at this node. Note the same biopsies also show endomysial and perimysial thickening attributed to the chronic neurogenic process, so this edge records where the finding is reported, not that denervation can be excluded as its cause.

evidence.snippet: Blood tests unveiled elevated creatine kinase (CK) levels in the majority of cases, with the highest value reaching up to 2400 U/L.
evidence.explanation: Gives the frequency and upper range of the creatine kinase elevation.

edges/21.description: Release of creatine kinase from damaged muscle fibres.

evidence.snippet: Of note, bilateral foot deformity was a very frequent feature revealed in almost 90% of the cases (15/17), ranging from pes cavus (65%, 11/17) to talipes equinovarus (35%, 6/17).
evidence.explanation: Gives the frequency of each deformity within the first cohort.

edges/22.description: Foot deformity develops in almost 90% of patients, the great majority before school age, in feet whose intrinsic and extrinsic muscles are unequally weakened.

evidence.snippet: In two independent cases, the foot deformities and tendon contractures were congenital suggesting antenatal onset of the disease.
evidence.explanation: Records the congenital instance of the deformity and what the authors infer from it about onset.

edges/23.description: The more severe end of the same deformity spectrum, congenital in two reported cases.

evidence.snippet: The mean age of symptom recognition was 2.0 ± 1.4 years with tip-toe walking, foot deformities, Achilles tendon contractures, and recurrent hip and patellar dislocations.
evidence.explanation: Names Achilles contracture among the presenting features and dates their recognition.

edges/24.description: Fixed shortening of the calcaneal tendon, present among the earliest recognised features.

evidence.snippet: The mean age of symptom recognition was 2.0 ± 1.4 years with tip-toe walking, foot deformities, Achilles tendon contractures, and recurrent hip and patellar dislocations.
evidence.explanation: Records tip-toe walking as a presenting feature alongside the contracture that produces it.

edges/25.description: Walking on the forefoot, the gait consequence of the contracture and of the dorsiflexor weakness.

evidence.snippet: One-third of the cases experienced frequent falls but despite the long disease course (median disease duration 36.5 years), only three members of the cohort (twins from Family 12 and index case from Family 6) had lost independent ambulation.
evidence.explanation: Gives the frequency of falls and, in the same sentence, the preserved ambulation that qualifies it.

edges/26.description: Frequent falls, reported in a third of the first cohort, in patients with weak ankles and fixed foot deformity.

evidence.snippet: We detected six different truncating variants in 15 affected individuals from six families of German, Arabic, and Roma descent.
evidence.explanation: Independent multi-family evidence for biallelic truncating VWA1 variants as the cause.

evidence.snippet: we identified 17 individuals from 15 families with an autosomal-recessive, non-length dependent, hereditary motor neuropathy and rare biallelic variants in VWA1
evidence.explanation: The concurrent, independently ascertained cohort establishing the same gene-disease relationship.

evidence.snippet: In humans, VWA1 (von Willebrand factor A domain containing 1) encodes a 445 amino acid ECM protein that is also referred to as von Willebrand factor A domain related protein (WARP).
evidence.explanation: Gives the protein length and the WARP synonym; the sentence restates established gene-product biology rather than reporting a new result.

evidence.snippet: Thanks to international cooperation between researchers, new genes have been implicated in dHMN, such as SORD and VWA1 .
evidence.explanation: A review of the family places VWA1 among its established causal genes.

genes/0.notes: Beyond the founder allele, the reported variant spectrum is dominated by truncating changes — stop-gains and frameshifts — with a small number of missense changes at proline residues. The second cohort reported 13 additional variants, 11 of them previously undescribed, 12 seen in compound heterozygosity and 8 of those in trans with the founder allele. A reciprocal 10 bp deletion at the same locus (c.62_71del10, p.G21Afs*12) is more common than the duplication in a Middle Eastern-enriched commercial cohort and was speculated by Pagnamenta et al. to be a second founder allele, but no biallelic case carrying it has been reported; it is recorded here as a lead, not as an established disease allele.

treatments/0.description: Rehabilitation aimed at the contractures and the gait. Achilles tendon contracture, foot plantar flexion, knee and hip flexion contractures are present in more than half of patients and appear early, so they are the component of the disease most open to non-pharmacological management.

treatments/1.description: Orthotic support for the bilateral foot drop that is the commonest functional problem. The device concept is carried as a qualifier because NCIT's Brace/Orthosis term is a medical device and is not reachable from Clinical Intervention or Procedure, so it cannot sit in the treatment_term slot.

treatments/2.description: Corrective surgery for the fixed foot deformities — talipes equinovarus in a third of patients, pes cavus in two thirds — and for the tendon contractures.

evidence.snippet: Reviewing previously unsolved exomes using lower QC filters may generate further diagnoses.
evidence.explanation: The concrete diagnostic recommendation this record exists to carry.

evidence.snippet: The study highlights the potential of lower quality control filters in exome analysis to enhance diagnostic yield of VWA1 disease that may account for up to 1% of unexplained hereditary neuropathies.
evidence.explanation: Independent restatement of the same recommendation with the yield it is expected to deliver.

treatments/3.description: Counselling for an autosomal recessive condition in which one allele is common enough in Western Europe that two unrelated carriers meeting is the usual genetic setting rather than consanguinity. The practical corollary is diagnostic: the founder duplication sits in a GC-rich repeat that standard exome pipelines under-call, so the authors of both original cohorts recommend targeted testing of VWA1 exon 1 and relaxed quality-control filters when re-analysing unsolved neuropathy exomes.

evidence.snippet: We speculate that a few findings of myopathic changes might be secondary to chronic denervation rather than indicating an additional myopathic disease process.
evidence.explanation: States the canonical position — the myopathic findings are read as a consequence of denervation, not as a second primary lesion.

evidence.snippet: Where data were available, immunohistochemical labelling for collagen VI appeared normal.
evidence.explanation: The collagen VI partner of WARP is normally deposited in patient muscle, which is the observation the secondary-myopathy model leans on: the matrix abnormality expected of a primary muscle-matrix disease was not found.

hypotheses/0.description: On this model the only primary lesion is in the peripheral nerve: loss of WARP from the nerve basement membrane causes motor axon loss, and every muscle finding — raised creatine kinase, myopathic motor units on needle EMG, dystrophic features on biopsy, fatty replacement on MRI — is a downstream consequence of long-standing denervation and reinnervation. Pagnamenta et al. argued this explicitly, noting that the histological features classically attributed to myopathy are also found in chronically denervated muscle, and that collagen VI immunolabelling was normal in the patient biopsies where it was assessed.

evidence.snippet: Myopathological and neurophysiological findings were indicative of combined neurogenic and myopathic pathology.
evidence.explanation: The cohort that named the condition a neuromyopathy states the combined pathology on which that name rests.

evidence.snippet: NEFM showed an increase in cells within the ECM in biopsies of all patients studied.
evidence.explanation: A muscle-matrix abnormality found in every patient biopsy examined, offered by that study as evidence bearing on primary muscle involvement.

evidence.snippet: Muscle magnetic resonance imaging showed a distinctive outside-in pattern of fatty replacement in the vastus lateralis, resembling that seen in type VI collagen-related myopathies.
evidence.explanation: An imaging pattern characteristic of a primary matrix myopathy rather than of denervation, in a muscle that is also a target of the collagen VI disorders WARP partners with.

hypotheses/1.description: On this model WARP loss injures the muscle directly, because WARP is a constituent of the muscle extracellular matrix as well as of the nerve basement membrane, so the disease is a neuromyopathy with two primary targets rather than a neuropathy with a denervated muscle. The Deschauer cohort named the condition a neuromyopathy on combined myopathological and neurophysiological grounds; a proteomic study of patient white blood cells, plasma and muscle set out explicitly to test for primary muscle vulnerability and reported extracellular accumulation of C-reactive protein and of NEFM in patient muscle; and muscle MRI in two independent reports shows an outside-in vastus lateralis pattern of the kind seen in collagen VI-related myopathy rather than the pattern expected of denervation.

evidence.snippet: Nevertheless, the true myopathic nature of the disease remained controversial, with some proposing a primarily neurogenic pathology and a secondary myopathic process.
evidence.explanation: States that the question is open and names both positions, which is exactly what this discussion records.

evidence.snippet: It is therefore possible that the preservation of the sartorius and gracilis muscles in SMA indicates a pathophysiologic mechanism involving direct muscle effects and may provide information useful for interpreting VUS.
evidence.explanation: The most recent argument for a direct muscle effect, from an imaging pattern rather than from histology.

evidence.snippet: Moreover, there is no common consent if the muscular affection is a secondary pathology based on vulnerability and dysfunction of motoric axons or if a primary muscle pathology is rather part of the clinical picture.
evidence.explanation: An independent statement that no consensus exists, from the group that set out to test the question.

open_questions/0.rationale:
The two cohorts that described the disease concurrently, in the same journal and the same year, named it differently, and the disagreement has not been resolved by any subsequent study. It is not a naming quibble: the answer determines whether the entity belongs with the motor neuropathies or with the muscular dystrophies for the purposes of gene-panel design, and it determines what a future therapy would have to reach.
For a secondary process: needle EMG was neurogenic in 10 of 12 studies and myopathic in a minority; four of seven biopsies were purely neurogenic; collagen VI immunolabelling was normal wherever assessed; the WARP-null mouse has no detectable skeletal muscle abnormality at all; and the histological features attributed to myopathy are known to occur in chronically denervated muscle.
For a primary process: WARP is expressed in skeletal muscle as well as nerve and binds collagen VI, whose own disorders are muscular dystrophies; creatine kinase is raised in most patients and reached 2400 U/L; muscle MRI in several patients shows an outside-in vastus lateralis pattern typical of collagen VI myopathy rather than of denervation; proteomics found increased C-reactive protein and NEFM in the extracellular space of patient muscle; and a whole-body MRI series in which gracilis and sartorius were spared in all five VWA1 patients reads that sparing as evidence for a direct muscle effect.
What would settle it: WARP immunostaining of patient muscle and nerve alongside quantitative matrix analysis, in patients whose denervation burden is measured independently; or a conditional muscle-restricted Vwa1 knockout. Neither has been reported.

evidence.snippet: Here, we report two cases from nonconsanguineous families in North America that presented in early childhood with lower extremity weakness and prominent foot deformities, and were found to carry bi-allelic variants in VWA1.
evidence.explanation: The report that introduced upper motor neuron signs into the phenotype, and its sample size.

evidence.snippet: WARP is expressed in the vasculature of neural tissues and in basement membrane structures of the peripheral nervous system.
evidence.explanation: Records the one piece of expression data that would make a central component biologically conceivable; it establishes vascular expression in neural tissue, not a corticospinal role.

open_questions/1.rationale: The first cohort recorded largely normal muscle tone and uniformly negative Babinski signs across its 17 patients. A subsequent two-child report made upper motor neuron signs its title finding, and the 20-patient cohort that followed recorded hyperreflexia, spasticity in two and upgoing plantars in two. No mechanism has been proposed. The possibilities are not distinguished by any published data: ascertainment drift as the phenotype widened, a genuine central component of a protein that is also expressed in the vasculature of neural tissues, or coincidence in a population where one causal allele is carried by roughly one person in 441 and so will sometimes be found alongside an unrelated condition. The third possibility is specifically worth testing for a disease whose defining allele is this common, and no report has excluded it.

open_questions/2.rationale:
The report's title names minipolymyoclonus, fasciculations and scapular winging in a novel VWA1 variant, and minipolymyoclonus is not currently curated in this entry at all. It cannot be curated from what is available: the record is a Letter, and `just fetch-reference PMID:41416782` returns `content_type: unavailable` with an empty body, so the only text obtainable is the title. A title is not a finding, and curating a phenotype from one would be exactly the fabrication the evidence SOP exists to prevent.
This is therefore filed as a task, not written in. Resolving it needs the full text: confirm that minipolymyoclonus was observed in a genetically confirmed patient, find the HP term for it, and check whether the fasciculations are tongue or limb. The scapular winging in the title is already curated from the 2024 cohort and needs no change.
Noted because minipolymyoclonus would be a genuinely new feature of the phenotype rather than a restatement — it is a sign of motor-unit loss and would attach to the same axon-loss node as the tongue fasciculations.

evidence.snippet: associated with serum aquaporin-4 immunoglobulin G antibodies
evidence.explanation: The NMOSD consensus criteria establish AQP4-IgG as the defining serologic marker for the AQP4-positive optic neuritis subgroup.

steps/0.description: In AQP4-IgG-positive NMOSD, optic neuritis reflects astrocyte-targeted autoimmunity with complement-mediated injury and secondary demyelination. This mechanism differs from primary MS-type demyelination and from MOGAD.

evidence.snippet: acute demyelinating optic neuritis
evidence.explanation: The randomized oral-versus-intravenous corticosteroid trial record specifically enrolled acute demyelinating optic neuritis.

evidence.snippet: measured as recovery of affected optic nerve conduction latency
evidence.explanation: RENEW used optic nerve conduction latency recovery as a remyelination endpoint, linking optic neuritis to demyelinating conduction delay.

steps/1.description: Many optic neuritis attacks are demyelinating optic neuropathies. Loss or dysfunction of optic nerve myelin slows visual pathway conduction and is reflected by prolonged visual evoked potential latency; retinal and optic nerve structural injury can be followed by OCT.

evidence.snippet: A rare inflammatory optic neuropathy
evidence.explanation: The Orphanet structured record anchors the isolated form as inflammatory optic neuropathy.

evidence.snippet: Autoimmune optic neuritis (ON) is a heterogeneous spectrum
evidence.explanation: The 2026 review supports heterogeneous immune-mediated etiologies for optic neuritis.

steps/2.description: Optic neuritis is driven by inflammatory injury within the optic nerve, producing acute or subacute visual dysfunction. The broad syndrome includes isolated inflammatory optic neuropathy as well as disease-specific immune mechanisms in MS, MOGAD, NMOSD, and systemic inflammatory disease.

evidence.snippet: Serum antibodies directed against myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein
evidence.explanation: International criteria establish serum MOG-IgG as the defining biomarker for MOGAD, a common optic neuritis etiology.

evidence.snippet: MOG-IgG-mediated demyelination occurs via complement-dependent cytotoxicity
evidence.explanation: The review describes antibody effector mechanisms relevant to MOGAD optic neuritis.

steps/3.description: In MOGAD-associated optic neuritis, antibodies to conformational MOG epitopes identify a demyelinating disease that is distinct from MS and AQP4-IgG NMOSD. MOG-IgG effector mechanisms include complement-dependent cytotoxicity, antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity, and T-cell supported CNS inflammation.

evidence.snippet: Visual function recovered faster in the group receiving intravenous methylprednisolone
evidence.explanation: ONTT supports high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone for faster visual recovery in acute optic neuritis.

evidence.snippet: bioequivalent doses of oral corticosteroids may be used as an alternative to IV corticosteroids
evidence.explanation: This randomized trial supports bioequivalent high-dose oral corticosteroids as an alternative route to high-dose IV therapy.

evidence.snippet: Oral prednisone alone, as prescribed in this study, is an ineffective treatment
evidence.explanation: The ONTT finding distinguishes high-dose steroid treatment from low-dose oral prednisone monotherapy.

treatments/0.description: High-dose corticosteroids, usually intravenous methylprednisolone or a bioequivalent high-dose oral regimen, accelerate recovery in acute optic neuritis. Low-dose oral prednisone alone, as used in the original ONTT, is not equivalent and increased new optic neuritis episodes.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: High-dose corticosteroids suppress acute inflammatory optic nerve injury and speed visual recovery.

evidence.snippet: PLEX+IVMP are more likely to improve EDSS after NMO relapses
evidence.explanation: This NMO/NMOSD relapse cohort supports adding plasma exchange to high-dose steroids, including relapses involving the optic nerves.

evidence.snippet: Most ON attacks improved with PLEX
evidence.explanation: The 395-attack international cohort supports PLEX as a clinically useful escalation therapy for severe optic neuritis and identifies delayed PLEX as a poor-outcome predictor.

evidence.snippet: PE may be beneficial as an escalating treatment
evidence.explanation: This severe optic neuritis case series supports plasma exchange as an escalation option when high-dose steroids are insufficient.

evidence.snippet: inadequate data to determine whether PLEX effectively treats acute ON
evidence.explanation: The systematic review supports clinical plausibility but cautions that definitive evidence for acute NMO/NMOSD optic neuritis remains limited.

treatments/1.description: Therapeutic plasma exchange is considered for severe or steroid-refractory optic neuritis, especially in NMOSD/AQP4-associated attacks. Evidence is strongest in observational NMO/NMOSD relapse cohorts, while aggregate data specific to acute NMO/NMOSD optic neuritis remain limited.

treatments/1/targets/0.description: Plasma exchange removes circulating pathogenic antibodies and complement mediators during severe antibody-associated attacks.

evidence.snippet: maintenance IVIG was associated with a reduction in disease relapse
evidence.explanation: This international adult MOGAD cohort supports maintenance IVIG as a relapse-prevention strategy relevant to relapsing MOG-associated optic neuritis.

treatments/2.description: Maintenance IVIG is used as a relapse-prevention option in relapsing MOGAD, including patients whose MOGAD phenotype includes optic neuritis. Evidence is retrospective and subtype-specific rather than a general treatment for all optic neuritis.

treatments/2/targets/0.description: IVIG is used to reduce relapsing MOG-IgG-associated inflammatory demyelinating attacks.

evidence.snippet: Adjudicated relapses occurred in 3 of 96 patients (3%) in the eculizumab group and 20 of 47 (43%) in the placebo group
evidence.explanation: The PREVENT trial supports eculizumab for relapse prevention in AQP4-IgG-positive NMOSD, including prevention of recurrent optic neuritis attacks in that subtype context.

treatments/3.description: Complement C5 blockade with eculizumab reduces relapse risk in AQP4-IgG-positive NMOSD; this is relevant to optic neuritis when optic nerve attacks occur as part of AQP4-IgG/NMOSD-associated disease.

treatments/3/targets/0.description: C5 blockade reduces terminal complement-mediated astrocyte injury in AQP4-IgG-positive NMOSD.

evidence.snippet: Compared with nonusers, OR for tobacco (> 20 g/d) adjusted for alcohol = 5.8 (CI = 3.1-10.9)
